part and a gravitational part — exactly as in standard physics. The segment density does not mix
with the kinematic Lorentz factor; it adds multiplicatively. This factorization is the mathematical
content of LLI preservation in SSZ.
Intuitively, the segment density is like the temperature in a room. Temperature is a scalar—it
has the same value regardless of which direction you face or how fast you walk through the room.
Likewise, Ξ has the same value at a given spacetime point regardless of the local frame of the
observer. The time-dilation factor D depends only on Ξ, which depends only on position, not on
the observer’s velocity or orientation. This suffices to guarantee LLI.
Why is this necessary? Without this proof, every prediction in the subsequent chapters would be
suspect. A theory that violates LLI at any level would produce frame-dependent observables that
contradict decades of precision measurements. By establishing LLI preservation at the outset of
Part II, we ensure that the kinematic framework is built on solid ground.
The frame-dragging discussion in Section 7.3 extends this analysis to rotating sources. In GR,
a rotating mass drags the local inertial frames around it (the Lense-Thirring effect). In SSZ, the

.1 Why Local Lorentz Invariance Matters
4.10.2 The Foundation of Modern Physics
Local Lorentz invariance is not merely one principle among many — it is the very foundation on
which both special relativity and general relativity are constructed. Every equation in the Standard
Model of particle physics, every prediction of quantum electrodynamics, and every calculation
in metric-perturbation astronomy presupposes LLI. Were LLI to be violated even slightly, the
consequences for our understanding of nature would be catastrophic.
To appreciate what LLI actually asserts, we can state it in precise language: the laws of physics
take exactly the same form in every local inertial (freely falling) reference frame,
irrespective of the frame’s velocity or orientation. This entails:
• A physicist working inside a closed laboratory cannot determine the laboratory’s velocity by
any internal experiment. Whether the lab moves at 0 km s￿¹ or at 200 000 km s￿¹ relative to
the Earth, all experiments performed inside yield identical results.
• The speed of light is the same in all directions, in all reference frames, at all times. This is the
most precisely tested prediction of LLI: the isotropy of light propagation has been confirmed
to parts in 10¹￿.
• The laws of electrodynamics, quantum mechanics, and thermodynamics are all Lorentz-
covariant—they transform correctly under Lorentz boosts and rotations.

LocalLorentzinvarianceisnotmerelyoneprincipleamongmany—itisthefoundationuponwhich
both Special and General Relativity are built. Every equation in the Standard Model of particle
physics, every prediction of quantum electrodynamics, and every calculation in metric-perturbation
astronomy assumes LLI. If LLI were even slightly violated, the consequences for our understanding
| of  | nature would | be  | catastrophic. |     |     |     |     |     |     |
| --- | ------------ | --- | ------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
169

To appreciate this, let us consider what LLI actually states. In precise language: The laws of
physics take the same form in every local inertial (freely falling) reference frame,
regardless of the velocity or orientation of the system. This means:
• A physicist in a closed laboratory cannot determine the laboratory’s velocity by any internal
experiment. Whether the lab moves at 0 km s−1 or 200 000 km s−1 relative to the Earth, all
|     | experiments |     | inside | yield | identical | results. |     |     |     |
| --- | ----------- | --- | ------ | ----- | --------- | -------- | --- | --- | --- |
• The speed of light is the same in all directions, in all reference frames, at all times. This is the
most precisely tested prediction of LLI: the isotropy of light propagation has been confirmed
|     | to  | parts | in 1018. |     |     |     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | ----- | -------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
• The laws of electrodynamics, quantum mechanics, and thermodynamics are all Lorentz-
covariant — they transform correctly under Lorentz boosts and rotations.

| 4.13.1  | Frame    | Dragging              | in GR | — Physical  | Background |     |     |
Framedraggingisoneofthemostdramaticpredictionsofgeneralrelativity: arotatingmassliterally
drags the surrounding spacetime, forcing nearby objects to co-rotate. The effect was predicted by
Josef Lense and Hans Thirring in 1918, barely three years after Einstein published GR.
Thephysicalpictureisvivid: imaginespacetimeasaviscousfluid. Arotatingmassislikeaspinning
ball immersed in this fluid — it drags the fluid along, creating a vortex-like flow pattern. Objects
near the spinning mass are carried along by this flow, even if they are trying to remain stationary.
The effect is called “gravitomagnetism” because it is analogous to the magnetic field produced by
| a moving | charge. |     |     |     |     |     |     |
| -------- | ------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 4.13.2    |     | Frame  | Dragging |     | in SSZ: | Segment | Advection |     |     |
In the Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) picture, the familiar frame-dragging effect of General Relativity
acquires a concrete, material interpretation. A rotating mass advects (carries along) the
surrounding segment lattice, i.e. the network of elementary volume elements that constitute the
spacetime fabric. Near the equatorial plane of a spinning body the segments acquire a tangential
displacement proportional to the spin parameter 𝑎; farther from the equator the displacement
vanishes. This differential advection creates a “segment vortex” (Segmentwirbel) that is the SSZ
| analogue |          | of the  | gravitomagnetic |         | vortex     | of GR. |     |     |     |

The material presented here is a puzzle piece of a larger theoretical edifice. No single chapter
contains the complete SSZ prediction for any observable; the full answer emerges only after
combining results from several chapters. Chapters 26–30 (the Validation chapters) demonstrate
how the various pieces are assembled in practice and compare the resulting predictions with
| experimental |     |     | data. |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |

and concepts introduced above. The logical dependency is strict: the equations for Ξ(𝑟), 𝐷(𝑟), and
the gravitomagnetic field are prerequisites for the derivations that follow. A reader who skips this

A common misunderstanding is to evaluate the results of this chapter in isolation, for example
by asking whether a single formula agrees with a particular data set. SSZ is a framework, not a
collection of independent equations. The true test is the systemic consistency of the entire set of
predictions, whichisverifiedinchapters26–30bymorethan145automatedtestsspanningmultiple
repositories. Only when the whole system passes these tests can we claim empirical adequacy.

Local Lorentz invariance (LLI) is the requirement that the laws of physics take exactly the same
form in every local inertial frame. It is one of the two pillars of General Relativity (the other being
the equivalence principle) and has been tested with extraordinary precision – current experimental

Spacetime (SSZ) framework introduced a preferred reference frame or broke the local Lorentz
symmetry, it would be immediately falsified by existing experimental data. The purpose of this
chapter is to demonstrate that SSZ exactly preserves LLI. The proof proceeds in three distinct
steps:

The second step of the proof shows that the modified time-dilation factor 𝐷 itself is invariant under

Finally, we verify that the numerical magnitude of Ξ allowed by SSZ is comfortably below the

4.16.2 Intuitive picture
It is helpful to think of the segment density Ξ in the same way we think of temperature in a room.
Temperature is a scalar: its value is the same regardless of the direction in which you look or
how fast you move through the room. Likewise, Ξ has a single value at a given spacetime event,
independent of the local reference frame of the observer.
Becausethetime-dilationfactor𝐷dependsonlyonΞ,andΞdependsonlyonposition,theresulting
time dilation is completely independent of the observer’s velocity or orientation. This independence
is sufficient to guarantee LLI.
4.16.3 Why this proof is essential
Without establishing LLI preservation, every prediction made in the subsequent chapters would be
suspect. A theory that violated LLI at any level would generate frame-dependent observables that
contradict decades of high-precision measurements. By securing LLI at the outset of Part II, we
ensure that the kinematic framework of SSZ rests on a solid foundation.

4.16.5 1. Why local Lorentz invariance matters
Local Lorentz invariance is the cornerstone that guarantees the universality of physical laws across
all freely falling observers. It underpins the very notion of a metric theory of gravity and ensures
thatexperimentalresultsarereproducibleregardlessofthelaboratory’sstateofmotion. Byproving
that SSZ respects LLI, we confirm that the theory can be meaningfully compared with, and tested
against, the wealth of precision data accumulated over the past century.
4.16.6 Experimental Bounds on LLI Violations
The most stringent contemporary limits on violations of local Lorentz invariance (LLI) arise from
three classes of precision experiments:
• Hughes–Drever experiments (nuclear-magnetic-resonance tests) bound any anisotropy of
inertia to the level of 10−24GeV.
• Michelson–Morley-type experiments employing rotating optical cavities constrain
directional variations of the speed of light to better than 10−18.
• Atomic-clock comparisons performed on rotating platforms limit anisotropies in time
dilation to the order of 10−22.
In the Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) framework these bounds are automatically satisfied. The field
Ξ (also written 𝑋𝑖) is a true scalar; it does not single out any spatial direction and therefore cannot
generate observable LLI-breaking effects. Importantly, the preservation of LLI in SSZ is exact,
not merely approximate: no matter how far experimental precision is pushed, a violation stemming
from the segment density cannot be detected. This exact symmetry is a structural consequence of
the theory rather than a result of fine-tuning.
4.16.7 The Equivalence Principle Argument
A second, independent line of reasoning for the exact conservation of LLI follows directly from the
equivalence principle. Consider a freely falling local inertial frame at some position r. To first
order in the neighbourhood of that point the segment density Ξ(r) is constant—by the equivalence
principle the local effects of gravity “disappear”. Consequently:
• All local experiments produce the standard results of special relativity.
• The speed of light is locally 𝑐 in every direction.
• Segments possess no preferred angular orientation at any point.
A non-zero gradient 𝜕Ξ/𝜕𝑟 does introduce a radial direction, but this is precisely equivalent to the

| 4.16.9   | The | Dragging  |          | of Gyroscope |     | Precession |     |
Frame dragging has two observable manifestations: the Lense-Thirring precession of orbital planes
(discussed above) and the geodetic precession of gyroscope spin axes. Gravity Probe B measured
| both effects | for | gyroscopes |     | in orbit | around | the Earth. |     |
| ------------ | --- | ---------- | --- | -------- | ------ | ---------- | --- |
The geodetic precession (also called de Sitter precession) is a consequence of the curvature of
spacetime around the Earth. It causes a gyroscope spin axis to precess by 6.6 arcseconds per
year in the plane of the orbit. This effect is independent of the Earth’s rotation and depends
only on the mass (through the Schwarzschild metric). In SSZ, the geodetic precession is modified
by the segment density: Omega_geodetic_SSZ = Omega_geodetic_GR times (1 + correction
of order Xi^2), where the correction is less than 10^{-18} for the Earth. The SSZ prediction is
| indistinguishable |     | from | GR  | for this | effect. |     |     |
| ----------------- | --- | ---- | --- | -------- | ------- | --- | --- |
The frame-dragging precession (Lense-Thirring) is caused by the rotation of the Earth and is much
smaller: approximately 0.039 arcseconds per year. Gravity Probe B measured this effect with a
precision of approximately 19 percent, confirming the GR prediction. The SSZ prediction differs
from GR by a factor of D = 1/(1 + Xi) approximately 1 - 7 times 10^{-10}, which is completely
| unmeasurable |     | with current |     | technology. |     |     |     |
| ------------ | --- | ------------ | --- | ----------- | --- | --- | --- |
The importance of these measurements for SSZ is not in discriminating between SSZ and GR (the
weak-field corrections are far too small) but in establishing the experimental framework for future
tests. The techniques developed for Gravity Probe B (cryogenic gyroscopes, drag-free satellites,
precision star trackers) will be essential for future strong-field tests of frame dragging around
compact objects. The SSZ prediction for frame-dragging near a neutron star (Xi approximately
0.1) differs from GR by approximately 10 percent, which could be measured by future pulsar timing
experiments that track the precession of pulsar spin axes in binary systems.
The most promising system for testing SSZ frame-dragging predictions is the double pulsar PSR
J0737-3039. This system consists of two pulsars orbiting each other with a period of 2.4 hours,
with significant spin-orbit coupling. The geodetic precession of the pulsar spin axis has already
been measured (by observing changes in the pulse profile as the spin axis precesses), and the
frame-dragging contribution to this precession could potentially be extracted with sufficient timing
precision.

4.17 Cross-References
4.17.1 Summary and Bridge to Chapter 8
Local Lorentz invariance (LLI) is not merely one principle among many; it is the very foundation
upon which both Special and General Relativity are built. Every equation in the Standard Model
of particle physics, every prediction of quantum electrodynamics, and every calculation in metric-
perturbation astronomy presupposes LLI. Were LLI to be violated even slightly, the consequences
for our understanding of nature would be catastrophic.
Toappreciatethis, letusstatepreciselywhatLLIasserts. Inexactlanguage: The laws of physics
take the same form in every local inertial (freely-falling) reference frame, regardless
of the frame’s velocity or orientation. This statement entails several concrete, experimentally
verified facts:
• A physicist working inside a sealed laboratory cannot determine the laboratory’s absolute
velocity by any internal experiment. Whether the lab moves at 0 km s−1 or 200 000 km s−1
relative to the Earth, all experiments performed within its walls yield identical results.
• The speed of light is the same in all directions, in all reference frames, at all times. This is the
most precisely tested prediction of LLI: the isotropy of light propagation has been confirmed
to parts in 1018.
• The laws of electrodynamics, quantum mechanics, and thermodynamics are all Lorentz-
covariant—they transform correctly under Lorentz boosts and rotations.
The proof presented in the preceding chapter demonstrates that Segmented Spacetime (SSZ)
preserves local Lorentz invariance exactly, thereby removing the most serious potential
objection to the framework. The argument relied on the scalar nature of the SSZ field Ξ and on
the local constancy of the function 𝐷(𝑟) within any sufficiently small region. By extending the
analysis to include frame-dragging effects, we showed that rotating sources do not introduce any
preferred direction, and the invariance holds for the full set of SSZ variables 𝜙, 𝑟 , 𝑠(𝑟), 𝑔 , and 𝑔 .
𝑠 1 2
4.17.2 Summary and Bridge to Chapter 8
Having secured the LLI proof, we can now turn to the first genuinely new kinematic prediction of
SSZ: the dual-velocity concept. Chapter 8 introduces two characteristic speeds associated with a
gravitating object—𝑣 (the escape velocity) and 𝑣 (the free-fall velocity). Because LLI has been
esc fall

demonstrated to hold in SSZ, these dual velocities are not artifacts of a hidden preferred frame;
they are genuine, observer-independent physical quantities that any experiment can, in principle,
measure.

4.18 Chapter 8: Dual Velocities — Escape, Fall, and Redshift
4.19 Summary
Every physics student learns about the escape velocity: the minimum speed required to leave a
gravitational field permanently. For Earth it is 11.2 km s−1; for the Sun’s surface 618 km s−1; at
the horizon of a black hole it equals the speed of light. This concept is universal, well-understood,
and identical in Newtonian gravity, General Relativity, and SSZ.
What is not universal — and what is unique to SSZ — is the notion of a dual velocity: the fall
velocity 𝑣 , defined as the reciprocal of the escape velocity through the relation
fall
𝑣 𝑣 = 𝑐2.
esc fall
This duality has no counterpart in standard GR. In GR a particle that falls from rest at infinity
arrives at radius 𝑟 with exactly the escape velocity, so the two speeds coincide. SSZ separates
them because the segment structure treats inward and outward motion asymmetrically: traversing
segments along the density gradient (inward) is physically different from traversing them against
the gradient (outward).
This chapter derives both velocities, proves the closure relation 𝑣 𝑣 = 𝑐2, shows how the duality
esc fall
is linked to the gravitational redshift, and examines the physical consequences at the Schwarzschild
radius.
Reader’s guide. Section 8.1 provides a detailed overview of the escape velocity. Section 8.2
introduces the fall velocity and explains the asymmetry. Section 8.3 derives the duality relation.

reduces the corresponding fall velocity so that their product remains locked at 𝑐2. This insight
opens the door to reformulating gravitational dynamics in terms of paired variables, much as
Hamiltonian mechanics does for position and momentum, and it may provide a useful bridge
between classical gravitation and quantum-like descriptions within the SSZ paradigm.

Falling is easier than escaping, not because of a force asymmetry, but because of a structural
asymmetry in the segment lattice. The constraint
𝑣 ×𝑣 = 𝑐2
esc fall
guarantees that this asymmetry does not violate energy conservation—it is a restriction, not a
source of free energy.
A helpful analogy for students is a moving walkway (escalator). Walking upward (escaping)
means fighting against the motion of the walkway, while walking downward (falling) is assisted by
it. The effort required to go upward multiplied by the ease of going downward remains constant; it
depends only on the walkway’s speed, not on your position on it. The segment lattice in SSZ plays
an analogous role: it creates an asymmetry between inward and outward motion while preserving
a fixed product of the two characteristic speeds.

4.23.6 Infalling Matter: The Velocity Decomposition
Chapter 23 develops a crucial application of the dual velocity structure: infalling matter near a
black hole can be decomposed into two components:
• v_fall component: The gravitationally absorbed velocity, channeled inward by the segment
gradient. This component does not produce radiation — it is “absorbed” by the segment
structure.
• v_eigen component: The intrinsic (proper) velocity of the matter, which persists after the
gravitational component is absorbed. This component does produce radiation — it is the
source of the radio waves and X-rays observed from accretion disks.
Thedecompositionv_total=v_fall+v_eigenisuniquetoSSZandprovidesanaturalexplanation
for why accreting black holes radiate: the matter’s intrinsic motion is not suppressed by the
gravitational field, only its coordinate fall velocity is affected by the segment structure.

4.25.4 Physical Origin of the Velocity Asymmetry
Why should escape and fall velocities differ? In Newtonian gravity, they are equal because the
gravitational potential is symmetric under time reversal: if a particle can fall from infinity to radius
rwithvelocityv,thenthesameparticlelaunchedwithvelocityvfromradiusrcanescapetoinfinity.
Time reversal symmetry guarantees v_esc = v_fall.
SSZ breaks this symmetry through the segment density gradient. A particle falling inward passes
through segments of increasing density, and each segment extracts a tiny amount of kinetic energy
(converting it to potential energy in the segment lattice). A particle escaping outward passes
through segments of decreasing density, and each segment returns a tiny amount of energy. But
the extraction and return are not symmetric: the extraction is proportional to Xi at the current
radius, while the return is proportional to Xi at the previous radius. Since Xi increases inward, the
extraction always exceeds the return, creating an asymmetry between inward and outward motion.
The asymmetry is small in the weak field (where Xi changes slowly with radius) and large in the
strong field (where Xi changes rapidly). At r = r_s, the asymmetry is maximal: v_fall is close
to c (the particle is falling nearly at light speed) while v_esc is much smaller (the particle must
overcome the maximum segment density). The product v_esc times v_fall = c^2 ensures that the
asymmetry does not violate energy conservation.
This physical picture provides intuition for the gravitational redshift. A photon emitted outward
from radius r starts with frequency f_emit and must climb through the segment lattice. Each
segmentextractsafractionofthephotonenergyproportionaltothelocalXi,reducingthefrequency.
The total frequency reduction is the integral of Xi along the path, which gives z = Xi(r_emit)
- Xi(r_obs) in the weak field. The photon does not retune (Chapter 15) – its local frequency
is unchanged – but the comparison between local frequency and infinity frequency shows the
accumulated effect of the segment lattice.
4.25.5 Connection to Orbital Mechanics
The dual velocities v_esc and v_fall have direct implications for orbital mechanics. The circular
orbital velocity at radius r is v_circ = sqrt(GM/r) in Newtonian gravity. In SSZ, the circular
orbital velocity is modified by the segment density: v_circ_SSZ = v_circ_Newton times 1/sqrt(1
+ Xi), which is slightly slower than the Newtonian value (because the segment density provides an
additional effective potential).
The ratio v_circ/v_esc characterizes the stability of circular orbits. In Newtonian gravity,
v_circ/v_esc = 1/sqrt(2) at all radii, and circular orbits are stable at all radii. In GR, the ratio
decreases with decreasing radius, and circular orbits become unstable inside the ISCO at r = 3 r_s.
In SSZ, the ratio behaves similarly to GR in the weak field but differs in the strong field: the ISCO
location is shifted by the segment density correction, and the transition from stable to unstable
orbits is modified by the blend function.
Forbinarypulsars(suchasPSRJ0737-3039ortheHulse-TaylorpulsarPSRB1913+16), theorbital
velocity is a few hundred km/s, corresponding to v/c of order 10^{-3}. At this velocity, the SSZ
correction to the orbital dynamics is of order Xi approximately 10^{-6}, which is measurable only
through accumulated effects (such as the orbital period decay due to metric perturbation emission).
The SSZ prediction for the orbital period decay agrees with GR to the precision of the current
measurements (approximately 0.1 percent for the Hulse-Taylor pulsar), consistent with the absence
of detectable SSZ corrections in the weak field.
202

For matter orbiting close to a compact object (such as the hot gas in the inner accretion disk of an
X-ray binary), the orbital velocity approaches c/sqrt(3) approximately 0.577 c at the ISCO. Here
the SSZ correction is significant: the orbital velocity at the SSZ-modified ISCO differs from the
GR value by approximately Xi(3 r_s) = r_s/(6 r_s) = 0.167, or about 17 percent. This correction
affects the observed properties of the inner accretion disk (temperature, luminosity, spectral shape)
and is in principle testable with high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy.
4.25.6 Energy Budget of Radial Infall
When a test particle falls radially from rest at infinity toward a compact object, its kinetic energy
increases as it accelerates. In Newtonian gravity, the kinetic energy at radius r is E_kin = GMm/r
= (1/2)mv_fall^2. In SSZ, the energy budget is modified by the segment density.
The total conserved energy of the particle is E = mc^2 (rest energy, since it starts from rest at
infinity). Atradiusr,theenergyisdistributedbetweenrestenergy,kineticenergy,andgravitational
potentialenergy: E=mc^2D(r)gamma_seg(r)=mc^2,whereD(r)=1/(1+Xi)isthegravitational
factor and gamma_seg includes both the gravitational and kinematic contributions.
Solving for the fall velocity: v_fall = c sqrt(1 - D^2) / D = c sqrt((1+Xi)^2 - 1) / (1+Xi) =
c sqrt(2Xi + Xi^2) / (1+Xi). In the weak field (Xi much less than 1), this reduces to v_fall
approximately c sqrt(2Xi) = sqrt(r_s c^2 / r) = sqrt(2GM/r), recovering the Newtonian result. In
the strong field (Xi approximately 0.802 at r_s), v_fall = c sqrt(2 times 0.802 + 0.644) / 1.802 =
c sqrt(2.248) / 1.802 = 0.832c.
For comparison, the GR fall velocity at r_s is v_fall_GR = c (in Schwarzschild coordinates) or c
sqrt(r_s/r) = c (at r = r_s). The SSZ fall velocity is 83.2 percent of c at the natural boundary
– fast but not light speed. This difference has consequences for the kinetic energy deposited when
accreting matter hits the natural boundary, affecting the thermal emission spectrum discussed in
Chapter 23.

4.28 Summary
The identity v_esc ⋅ v_fall = c2 is an exact kinematic closure condition unique to SSZ. Chapter
8 introduced the dual velocities and derived their product algebraically. This chapter goes deeper:
it places the closure in the context of other constant-product relations in physics, explores its
physical meaning as an information-conservation law, proves its regime independence, derives its
consequences for the black hole information problem, and connects it to the broader structure of
SSZ kinematics.
The closure is more than a mathematical curiosity. It is a structural constraint on the SSZ
framework — any modification to the velocity definitions that broke the closure would signal an
internal contradiction. It is also a testable prediction: the physical separation of v_esc and
v_fall into distinct observables (Chapter 23) depends on the closure being exact, not approximate.
Reader’s guide. Section 9.1 provides the formal derivation with worked examples. Section 9.2
places the closure in the context of constant-product relations in physics. Section 9.3 explores the
physical meaning in terms of information conservation. Section 9.4 proves regime independence.
Section 9.5 discusses implications for the black hole information problem. Section 9.6 summarizes
validation.
205

Why is this necessary? Each chapter in this book serves a specific function in the derivation chain
that connects the SSZ axioms (phi-geometry, segment density, two-regime structure) to falsifiable
predictions. This chapter – Kinematic Closure — v_esc ⋅ v_fall = c2 – addresses a question that
cannot be answered by the preceding chapters alone and whose answer is required by subsequent
chapters. The material is presented at a level accessible to third-semester physics students, with
explicit motivation for every step and clear statements of what is assumed versus what is derived.

In every case above, the constant product arises from a duality — two complementary descriptions

The SSZ closure suggests that v_esc and v_fall are gravitational duals — conjugate kinematic
variables that encode complementary aspects of the gravitational interaction. Escape velocity
measures the “outward resistance” of the field (how hard it is to leave). Fall velocity measures
the “inward response” of the segment lattice (how the lattice accommodates infall). Together, they
completely characterize the gravitational state at any radius — knowing either one immediately

4.30.2 Connection to the Black Hole Information Problem
The black hole information paradox is one of the deepest unresolved problems in theoretical physics.
In GR, information that falls into a black hole disappears behind the event horizon and (according
to Hawking’s semiclassical calculation) is eventually destroyed when the black hole evaporates.
This contradicts the fundamental principle of quantum mechanics that information is conserved
(unitarity).
SSZ offers a potential solution through the kinematic closure. Because

This is not a complete resolution of the information problem (which requires a full quantum-
gravitational treatment), but it eliminates the kinematic aspect of the paradox: the SSZ framework

Intuitively, this means: the material in this chapter provides one piece of a larger puzzle. No single
chapter contains the complete SSZ prediction for any observable – that requires combining results
across multiple chapters. The validation chapters (26-30) show how this combination works in
practice and compare the resulting predictions with experimental data.
The next chapter, Maxwell Waves as Rotating Space, builds directly on the results established here.
The logical dependency is strict: the formulas and concepts introduced above are prerequisites for
what follows. A reader who skips this chapter will encounter undefined quantities in subsequent
derivations.
A common misinterpretation would be to evaluate the results of this chapter in isolation – for
instance, asking whether a single formula alone matches the data. SSZ is a framework, not a set
of independent equations. The consistency of the overall system is the test, not the agreement
of individual expressions. This systemic consistency is what Chapters 26-30 verify through 145

5.11.3 SSZ Geometric Interpretation
InSSZtheelectricandmagneticfieldsacquireageometricinterpretationthroughtheunderlying
segment structure of spacetime.
Electric field E: E represents a radial distortion of the segment boundaries. As an
electromagnetic wave traverses a region of spacetime, the segment boundaries are displaced
radially—compressed on the side the wave entered and stretched on the opposite side. The
magnitude of E is equal to the amplitude of this radial displacement.
Magnetic field B: B represents a tangential (rotational) distortion of the segment
boundaries. The segment boundaries are twisted within the plane that is orthogonal to the
direction of propagation. The magnitude of B corresponds to the amplitude of this twist.
The central structural requirement is that E and B are always perpendicular to each
other and to the propagation direction. In SSZ this is not an empirical observation that
“happens to be true’’; it is a topological necessity. The segment boundaries are two-dimensional
239

surfaces, and the only deformations that preserve their connectivity are radial shifts and tangential
rotations in the plane orthogonal to the propagation direction. Any other deformation would tear
the segment lattice apart.
This topological argument deserves emphasis because it explains one of the deepest properties
of electromagnetism: the transversality of electromagnetic waves. In conventional physics
transversality follows from the divergence-free condition for E and B in vacuum. In SSZ it follows
directly from the two-dimensional nature of the segment boundaries. Both approaches yield the
same result, but the SSZ reasoning supplies a geometric origin rather than a purely algebraic
condition.
The scaling factor
𝑠(𝑟) = 1+Ξ(𝑟)
introduced in Chapter 10 modifies the amplitude of these distortions. In regions of higher segment
density the same physical distortion corresponds to a larger field strength because the segments
are more tightly packed. Consequently, the electromagnetic field energy increases in strong
gravitational fields: the same rotational amplitude carries more energy per unit volume in denser
segment regions.
Thus, the SSZ picture unifies the ray-tracing description of geometric optics with a concrete
geometric picture of the fields themselves, linking the segment-counting language of Chapter 12,
the scaling factor 𝑠(𝑟), and the topological constraints that enforce the familiar transverse nature
of light.

5.11.6 Gravitational Birefringence
In an anisotropic medium, different polarization states propagate at different speeds, producing
birefringence (double refraction). The SSZ segment lattice in a spherically symmetric field is
isotropic (Ξ depends only on 𝑟, not on direction), so no birefringence occurs for radial or tangential
propagation. However, for oblique propagation (at an angle to the radial direction) the effective
refractive index depends on the propagation direction relative to the Ξ-gradient, potentially
introducing a weak birefringence.

5.11.7.1 SSZ’s complementary picture
SSZaddsageometric substratetothisstandarddescription. IntheSSZview,anelectromagnetic
wave can be regarded as a rotational distortion of the local segment structure:
• the electric field corresponds to a radial stretching (or dilation) of the individual segments,
and
• the magnetic field corresponds to a tangential twisting (or shear) of those same segments.
The propagation of the wave is then the propagation of this rotational distortion through
the segment lattice. In other words, the wave does not travel as a separate field on a background
spacetime; it travels as a pattern of successive segment deformations that respect the underlying
lattice connectivity.
5.11.7.2 No replacement of the Maxwell description
This geometric picture does not replace the standard Maxwell formulation; it supplements it.
All practical calculations throughout this book are performed with the familiar Maxwell equations,
exactly as in General Relativity (GR) or in flat spacetime. The SSZ interpretation is introduced
solely to provide physical intuition about why electromagnetic waves possess the properties they
do—transversality, twoindependentpolarizations, and propagation at speed c in vacuum—andhow
those properties may be modified in strong gravitational fields where the segment geometry
is significantly warped.
5.11.7.3 Intuitive analogy
Imagine a row of springs connected end-to-end. A transverse wave moves along the row because
each spring displaces its neighbor sideways. In the SSZ framework, the segments play
the role of those springs: they transmit the electromagnetic distortion from one to the next.
The transversality of electromagnetic waves follows from the fact that only rotational
(transverse) distortions can propagate through the segment lattice; a longitudinal
distortion would attempt to compress or tear the segments, which the lattice structure forbids.

5.15 Historical Context
The geometric interpretation of electromagnetism has several historical precedents. Kaluza
(1921) derived the Maxwell equations from five-dimensional general relativity, showing that
electromagnetism can emerge from a higher-dimensional metric. Klein (1926) subsequently
introduced the idea of compactifying the extra dimension, thereby explaining why the fifth
dimension is not observed at macroscopic scales. Wheeler (1955) proposed the famous “charge-
without-charge” concept, in which electric charge arises from non-trivial spacetime topology rather
than from point-like sources. Hestenes (1966) later employed the bivector formalism of geometric
248

algebra to represent the electromagnetic field, providing a compact algebraic description of the
electric and magnetic components.
The Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) interpretation with rotating segments is fundamentally
different from these earlier approaches. It does not require any additional spatial dimensions,
it does not rely on topological trapping of field lines, and it does not invoke self-gravitating
configurations of the field. In SSZ, the electric (E) and magnetic (B) fields appear as orthogonal
components of a local segment-boundary rotation that exists entirely within ordinary 3 +
1 dimensional spacetime. The bivector formalism of geometric algebra maps directly onto the
rotation plane defined by each segment, so the mathematical structure aligns naturally with the
physical picture.
In the weak-field regime the rotating-segment picture is experimentally indistinguishable from
standard electrodynamics; all measured quantities—such as the Lorentz force, wave propagation
speed, and energy-momentum transfer—coincide with the predictions of Maxwell’s theory. In the
strong-field regime the SSZ model introduces a modification of the rotation amplitude through the
scalar function
𝑠(𝑟) = 1+Ξ,
where Ξ (the SSZ scalar) depends on the local curvature of spacetime. This alteration leads to
the same Shapiro time delay and light-deflection effects that were derived in Chapters 10 and 12,
but it does so via a different physical mechanism: the enhanced segment rotation rather than a
curvature-induced change in the metric alone.
Thus,theSSZinterpretationisfullyconsistentwithallexistingobservations,yetitdoesnotgenerate
independent, falsifiable predictions beyond those already accounted for by conventional theory. Its
primaryvalueliesinprovidingaconcretephysicalintuition—visualizingelectromagneticphenomena
as rotations of spacetime segments—rather than in delivering novel empirical consequences.
5.15.1 Connection to Photon Spin
The geometric interpretation of electromagnetism has a long lineage. Kaluza (1921) derived the
Maxwell equations from a five-dimensional formulation of relativity. Klein (1926) subsequently
compactifiedthefifthdimension,providingthefirstconcretemechanismforhidingextradimensions.
Wheeler (1955) introduced the idea of “charge without charge’’ by exploiting non-trivial spacetime
topology, and Hestenes (1966) showed how bivectors of geometric algebra can be used to represent
the electromagnetic field in a coordinate-free way.
The Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) interpretation with rotating segments departs fundamentally from
theseearlierapproaches. Itdoes notinvokeadditionalspatialdimensions, itavoidsanytopological
confinement, and it does not rely on self-gravitating field configurations. In SSZ the electric E and
magnetic B fields appear as orthogonal components of the local segment-boundary rotation
in ordinary 3 + 1 dimensions. The bivector formalism of geometric algebra maps directly onto
this plane of rotation, so that the familiar field tensor emerges as the projection of the underlying
rotational bivector onto spacetime.
In the weak-field limit the rotating-segment picture is experimentally indistinguishable from
standard electrodynamics; all measured quantities—wave propagation speed, impedance, radiation
patterns—coincide with the predictions of Maxwell’s theory. In the strong-field regime the factor

𝑠(𝑟) = 1+Ξ
modifies the amplitudes of the local rotations. This modification generates the Shapiro delay and
the gravitational light-deflection derived in Chapters 10 and 12, without invoking a separate

because it reproduces the same measurable outcomes as conventional theory, it is not independently

rather than a source of novel testable predictions.

5.15.2 Connection to Photon Spin
The photon’s intrinsic spin (helicity ±1) maps naturally onto the rotation direction of the segment
boundaries. Left-circular polarization corresponds to a counter-clockwise rotation of the local
segment lattice, while right-circular polarization corresponds to a clockwise rotation. Linear
polarization is simply a superposition of the two opposite rotation senses. This correspondence
preserves the full algebra of standard polarization states and supplies a concrete geometric picture:
a photon’s polarization state is the rotation state of the segment-lattice disturbance it carries.
Within the SSZ framework the spin-helicity relationship is encoded in the same bivector that
describesEandB. Thebivector’shandednessdeterminesthesignofthehelicity,andthemagnitude
oftherotationamplitudeismodulatedbythefactor𝑠(𝑟). Consequently, phenomenasuchasoptical
activity in a curved segment lattice or spin-dependent phase shifts can be understood as variations
of the underlying rotational geometry, rather than as separate quantum-field effects. This unified
description reinforces the view that SSZ provides a coherent geometric substrate for both classical
electromagnetism and the quantum-mechanical spin properties of light.

Electromagnetic waves possess two independent polarisation states (right-hand circular and left-
hand circular, or equivalently horizontal and vertical linear polarisation). In the SSZ segment
picture these two orthogonal polarisation states correspond to two independent rotational modes of
| the local | segment | lattice. |     |     |     |     |     |

• A right-hand circularly polarised wave rotates the segments clockwise when observed

| same | observation. |     |     |     |     |     |     |
| ---- | ------------ | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
252

Linear polarisation is simply the superposition of these two opposite rotational modes.
Thesegmentpictureexplainswhyexactlytwopolarisationstatesexist: athree-dimensionalsegment
lattice has precisely two independent rotational degrees of freedom that are perpendicular to any
given propagation direction. A third mode—rotation in the plane that contains the propagation
direction—would correspond to a longitudinal wave. Such a longitudinal mode is forbidden by the
lattice structure, as discussed earlier in the book.
In a gravitational field the spatial gradient of the segment density can introduce a coupling between
the two circular-polarisation modes. This coupling manifests as gravitational Faraday rotation:
the plane of linear polarisation rotates while the wave travels through a region where the SSZ field
Ξ varies. SSZ predicts this effect, but a quantitative calculation has not yet been carried out. It
remains one of the open problems identified in Chapter 29.

This picture gives a clear physical explanation for the gravitational slowing of light. In a
gravitational field the segment lattice becomes denser (the value of the SSZ parameter Ξ
increases). A higher Ξ means a larger effective inertia per unit volume, so the rotational
disturbances that represent the electromagnetic field are forced to move more slowly. The result is
a reduced propagation speed 𝑐𝐷(𝑟), directly analogous to the way sound waves travel more slowly
in a denser medium.
Thus, the Poynting vector not only quantifies electromagnetic energy flow, it also serves as the
conduit through which segment-momentum is transferred, linking the macroscopic behaviour of
light to the microscopic structure of the SSZ lattice.

or expand them. This geometric fact is the origin of the transversality condition.

| 5.21 | Summary |     |               |     |     |       |          |
How fast does light travel through a gravitational field? In general relativity, the answer depends
on the coordinate system — the “coordinate speed of light” is a gauge-dependent quantity with no
direct physical meaning. What IS physically meaningful is the group velocity: the speed at which
a wave packet (and the information it carries) propagates from emitter to detector.
SSZ provides a first-principles derivation of the group velocity from the discrete structure of the
segment lattice. A photon traverses segments one at a time, spending a fixed proper time in each
258

Figure 5.4: Fig 12.1
259

segment. The resulting group velocity v_group = c $￿$D(r) — more precisely, the physical radial
velocity d￿/dt (see Ch. 33 bridge identity) — emerges not as an assumption but as a counting result
— the number of segments traversed per unit coordinate time. This chapter derives the formula,
explains the physical mechanism, discusses the absence of gravitational dispersion, and provides
worked examples for Solar System and strong-field scenarios.

5.21.1 Pedagogical Overview
The speed of light in vacuum is exactly
𝑐 = 299792458 m/s,
by definition since 2019, when the metre was re-defined in terms of the speed of light. But what
does “the speed of light” mean when a gravitational field is present?
In the theory of General Relativity (referred to as ART in the German literature), the answer
depends on the chosen coordinate system. In Schwarzschild coordinates the coordinate speed of
light for radial propagation,

meaningful quantity—it is an artefact of the coordinate choice. The locally measured speed of light
is always 𝑐 in any coordinate system, as guaranteed by local Lorentz invariance (LLI).
In the Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) framework the coordinate speed of light is expressed as

the Shapiro delay (the extra time light needs to travel past a massive object) and contributes to
the deflection of light.

Intuitively, each segment of spacetime can be thought of as a speed bump on a road. The local
speed limit—𝑐—is the same everywhere, but the density of speed bumps varies with position. In
regionsofhighsegmentdensity(closetoamass)therearemorebumpsperunitcoordinatedistance,
so the coordinate travel time is longer. This is the physical mechanism behind the Shapiro delay:
light takes longer to traverse a region of high segment density not because it slows down locally,
| but because | there are | more | segments | to  | cross. |     |     |

Instead of evaluating a coordinate-dependent integral as in ART, SSZ simply counts the number of
segments along the light path and multiplies by the local traversal time per segment. The resulting
prediction agrees with the post-Newtonian (PPN) result to the same accuracy, but the physical
| picture  | is far more    | transparent. |          |     |                 |     |       |

5.21.4 SSZ’s Answer
SSZ supplies the underlying mechanism: light is observed to travel more slowly because it must
pass through a larger number of densely packed spacetime segments. Each individual segment
crossing consumes exactly the same local proper time, but in a gravitational field the segments
appear compressed when viewed from a distant observer’s coordinate system. Consequently the
coordinate-space velocity of a photon is reduced according to

5.21.4.1 Intuitive picture
Think of every spacetime segment as a speed bump on a road. A car that drives over a road littered
with speed bumps reaches its destination more slowly than a car on a perfectly smooth highway,
not because the car’s engine is weaker, but because each bump imposes a finite time penalty. In
the same way, a photon that traverses regions where the segments are more tightly packed appears
to move more slowly when expressed in the distant observer’s coordinates. The local speed of light
never changes—it remains exactly 𝑐 in the photon’s own inertial frame—but the coordinate time
required to cover a given radial interval grows because a larger number of segment crossings must
be completed per unit distance.
This counting-based slowdown is precisely the physical origin of the Shapiro time delay: the extra
coordinate time accrued by the photon is nothing more than the sum of the tiny proper-time
intervals spent crossing each compressed segment along its path.

5.22.2 Physical Interpretation
The group-velocity formula has a transparent interpretation, and in the standard flat-spacetime
case (Ξ = 0) it reduces to v_group = c.
• In flat spacetime (Ξ = 0): v_group = c. Standard case.
• Near the Sun’s surface (Ξ ≈ 2 × 10￿￿): v_group ≈ c(1 - 2 × 10￿￿). Light is slower by
~0.6 m/s.
• At a neutron star surface (Ξ ≈ 0.15): v_group ≈ 0.87c. Light is 13 % slower.
• At the SSZ natural boundary (Ξ = 0.802): v_group = 0.555c. Light travels at 55.5 %
of its vacuum speed.
The segment-counting mechanism provides the physical explanation that GR lacks: light slows
because the segment lattice is denser, and each segment requires a fixed proper time to traverse.

5.30.5 Comparison with Alternative Gravity Theories
Several alternative theories of gravity predict modifications to the speed of light in a gravitational
field. It is instructive to compare the SSZ prediction with these alternatives:
Brans-Dicketheory: thecoordinatespeedoflightisc_BD=c(1-(1+omega_BD^{-1})r_s/(2r)),
whereomega_BDistheBrans-Dickecouplingparameter. Foromega_BDapproachinginfinity, this
reduces to the GR result. The Cassini mission constrains omega_BD to be greater than 40,000,
making the Brans-Dicke correction undetectable in the solar system.
TeVeS (Tensor-Vector-Scalar theory, Bekenstein 2004): predicts different coordinate speeds for
electromagnetic and metric perturbations, violating the equivalence of photon and graviton
propagation. This prediction was dramatically tested and ruled out by the simultaneous detection
of metric perturbations and gamma rays from the neutron star merger GW170817/GRB170817A,
which showed that the two speeds agree to within 10^{-15}.
SSZ: the coordinate speed of light is c_SSZ = c/(1 + Xi), and the metric perturbation speed is also
c/(1 + Xi) (because metric perturbations are also distortions of the segment lattice). SSZ therefore
predicts equal speeds for electromagnetic and metric perturbations, consistent with GW170817.
This is a non-trivial consistency check: the SSZ framework could have predicted different speeds
for the two types of waves, but it does not.
The GW170817 observation is one of the strongest constraints on modifications to metric
perturbation propagation. SSZ passes this constraint automatically because the scaling factor
s(r) applies to all wave modes (electromagnetic and gravitational) equally. This equality is a
consequence of the universality of the segment lattice: all fields propagate through the same lattice
and experience the same effective refractive index.
5.30.6 The Coordinate Speed of Light and Causality
A common concern about modifications to the speed of light in a gravitational field is whether they
violate causality. If the physical radial velocity of light is 𝑐/𝑠(𝑟) = 𝑐⋅𝐷(𝑟) in coordinate time, does
this mean that signals can travel faster or slower than 𝑐 in a way that creates causal paradoxes?
The answer is no. The quantity 𝑐/𝑠(𝑟) = 𝑑ℓ/𝑑𝑡 is a coordinate-dependent quantity that has
no direct physical meaning; itisreferencedtothecoordinatetimeratherthantothepropertime
of a local observer. The physical speed of light—the speed measured by any local observer using
local clocks and rulers—is always exactly 𝑐, regardless of the gravitational field. The coordinate
speed differs from 𝑐 because the coordinate clocks and rulers are affected by the gravitational field
(they are not the local clocks and rulers of a freely falling observer).
This distinction between coordinate speed and local speed is the same in SSZ as in GR. In
Schwarzschild coordinates, the coordinate speed of radial light in GR is

5.33 Summary
When a photon traverses a gravitational field, its total travel time exceeds the geometric (straight-
line, flat-spacetime) prediction. In GR, this excess is the Shapiro delay — one of the four classical
tests of general relativity. The standard GR calculation involves integrating the null geodesic
equation through the curved metric, yielding a result that mixes geometric and gravitational
contributions in a non-separable way.
SSZ reveals a simpler structure: the total travel time decomposes additively into a geometric
component (the flat-spacetime travel time) and a segment component (the excess time from
traversing denser segments). This decomposition is exact in SSZ, not an approximation. It provides
computational advantages, physical insight, and a natural explanation for why gravitational time
delays from multiple sources should combine linearly — a superposition principle for gravitational
optics.
This chapter derives the additive decomposition from the group velocity formula (Chapter 12),
demonstrates its equivalence to the standard Shapiro delay (with PPN correction), shows how
it simplifies multi-source calculations, and provides worked examples for Solar System and
astrophysical scenarios.
Reader’s guide. Section 13.1 motivates the decomposition. Section 13.2 derives it from the group
velocity. Section 13.3 connects to Shapiro delay. Section 13.4 discusses the superposition principle.
Section 13.5 provides worked examples. Section 13.6 summarizes validation.
Why is this necessary? Each chapter in this book serves a specific function in the derivation chain
that connects the SSZ axioms (phi-geometry, segment density, two-regime structure) to falsifiable
predictions. Thischapter–AdditiveDecompositionofLightTravelTime–addressesaquestionthat
cannot be answered by the preceding chapters alone and whose answer is required by subsequent
chapters. The material is presented at a level accessible to third-semester physics students, with
explicit motivation for every step and clear statements of what is assumed versus what is derived.

The additive decomposition offers practical advantages for multi-source calculations. Suppose
several signals from different astrophysical sources all skim the same massive body. In SSZ the

GR, by contrast, each source requires a separate coordinate integration, since the decomposition

| 5.36.2  | Comparison  | with         | GR            |     |               |     |     |
In General Relativity the multi-body Shapiro delay is not simply additive. The metric for
several masses cannot be obtained by a linear superposition of individual Schwarzschild metrics;
instead, nonlinear gravitational interactions couple the contributions of the different bodies. In the
Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) framework the superposition principle holds because the quantityΞ
enters linearly in the group-velocity formula. Consequently, the total delay can be written as a
sum of the individual segment delays,Ξ _total=￿Ξ _i, in the weak-field regime. In strong fields
this linear approximation may break down, and higher-order corrections to the simple sum become
| necessary | (see Chapter29       | on the | multi-body |     | problem). |     |     |
| --------- | -------------------- | ------ | ---------- | --- | --------- | --- | --- |
| 5.36.3    | Pulsar-Timing-Arrays |        |            |     |           |     |     |
Pulsar-Timing-Arrays (PTAs) search for metric perturbations by monitoring the arrival times of
millisecond-pulsar signals. Eachpulsar signal traverses the gravitational potentialof the Milky Way
and accumulates a segment delay. The SSZ decomposition predicts that this delay is additive over
all mass concentrations along the line of sight, which greatly simplifies the timing model compared
| with a | full nonlinear | ART (General |     | Relativistic) | calculation. |     |     |
| ------ | -------------- | ------------ | --- | ------------- | ------------ | --- | --- |
The practical impact of this additive correction is small for current PTAs—the correction lies below
the present timing precision. However, next-generation PTAs that will operate with the Square
Kilometre Array are expected to reach the sensitivity required to distinguish between the additive
| SSZ model | and the  | fully nonlinear, | non-additive |     | delay models. |     |     |
| --------- | -------- | ---------------- | ------------ | --- | ------------- | --- | --- |
| 5.36.4    | Physical | Interpretation   |              |     |               |     |     |
The superposition principle has a deep physical meaning. In SSZ, each mass contributes
independently to the local segment density. A photon traversing the combined field of Sun and
Jupiter experiences the total segment density Xi_Sun(r) + Xi_Jupiter(r) at each point. Since the
group velocity depends on the total Xi, and since the integral of a sum is the sum of integrals, the
| delay from | each mass | separates | cleanly. |     |     |     |     |
| ---------- | --------- | --------- | -------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
283

Thisisanalogoustoelectrostatics,wherethepotentialfrommultiplechargesisthesumofindividual
potentials (because Poisson’s equation is linear). In SSZ, the segment density plays the role of the
gravitational potential, and the linearity of Xi-superposition in the weak field produces additive
time delays.
The analogy breaks down in the strong field, where Xi_total is no longer a simple sum of individual
contributions. The multi-body problem in SSZ remains open (Chapter 29), and the superposition
principle must be treated as a weak-field result until a nonlinear extension is developed.
| 5.36.5 | Observational |     | Consequences |     |     |     |     |     |     |
| ------ | ------------- | --- | ------------ | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The superposition principle has practical consequences for precision astrometry. The European
Space Agency’s Gaia mission measures stellar positions with microarcsecond precision, requiring
light-time corrections for every Solar System body along each line of sight. If the SSZ superposition
principle is exact, these corrections can be computed independently for each body and summed
— a significant computational simplification over the full nonlinear GR calculation. For Gaia’s
precision level, the difference between linear superposition and full GR is below the noise floor, so
| the principle | is      | operationally |         | valid.  |       |     |     |     |     |

| 5.41.3    | Practical |        | Advantage: | Multi-Source |     |     | Calculations |     |
Consider an observer who monitors three pulsars whose radio beams all pass in the immediate
vicinity of the same neutron star. In the standard relativistic theory (ART, i.e. General Relativity),
the propagation time of each pulse must be obtained from a separate four-dimensional line integral
along its null geodesic. In the Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) framework, the contribution of the
neutron star to the total segment delay can be evaluated a single time—as an integral of the fieldΞ
(Xi) along a purely radial profile—and then transferred to each individual ray by means of a purely
geometric correction factor that depends only on the impact parameter (b). This factorisation
reduces the computational effort from three full space-time integrations to one one-dimensional
| radial integration |     | plus | three inexpensive |     | geometric |     | corrections. |     |
| ------------------ | --- | ---- | ----------------- | --- | --------- | --- | ------------ | --- |
For pulsar-timing arrays—such as the International Pulsar Timing Array that is used to search for
low-frequency metric perturbations—this separation can dramatically accelerate the data-analysis
pipeline. The timing residuals recorded by a PTA contain correlated Shapiro-like delays produced
by many gravitating bodies (the Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, etc.). Because SSZ provides an additive
decomposition of the total delay, the contribution of each body can be computed independently
(again as a radial Ξ-integral) and then summed, eliminating the need to recompute the full four-
| dimensional | integral |     | for every | source-receiver |     | pair. |     |     |
| ----------- | -------- | --- | --------- | --------------- | --- | ----- | --- | --- |
Thus, multi-source calculations that are prohibitively expensive in ART become tractable in SSZ,
opening the way to real-time modelling of large timing-array data sets.

The additive decomposition can be stated precisely as follows. The total coordinate travel time for
| a light | ray from point | A   | to point   | B along |       | path P is: |     |     |

| T(A, B) | = T_geo(A,     | B)  | + T_seg(A, |         | B, P) |            |     |     |
where T_geo = integral of dl/c is the geometric travel time (independent of the gravitational field)
and T_seg = integral of Xi(r) dl/c is the segment delay (dependent on the gravitational field along
the path).
The geometric term T_geo depends only on the endpoints A and B and the path geometry. For
a straight-line path, T_geo = |AB|/c. For a bent path (as occurs when light is deflected by a

The segment term T_seg depends on the segment density profile along the path. For a radial path

includes both the radial and angular components of Xi along the path. The full expression,

equally to the light deflection and Shapiro delay, as discussed in Chapter 10.
The additive structure has a deep mathematical origin: it follows from the linearity of the scaling
factor s(r) = 1 + Xi(r). Because s is linear in Xi, the integral of s along the path separates into
a Xi-independent part (the 1) and a Xi-dependent part (the Xi). If s were a nonlinear function
of Xi (as in some alternative gravity theories), the decomposition would not be additive, and the
| multi-source | computational |     | advantage        |     | would | be lost. |      |        |

The SSZ prediction differs from GR for strong-field lenses – hypothetical configurations where the
light path passes close to the Schwarzschild radius of the lens. For such configurations, the segment
density Xi becomes significant, and the strong-field Xi formula must be used. The predicted time
delay correction is of order Xi^2 relative to the GR value, which is less than 10^{-10} for all known
gravitational lenses.
Gravitational lensing time delays have been measured for several multiply-imaged quasars (e.g.,
Q0957+561, B1608+656, RXJ1131-1231). These measurements are used to determine the Hubble
constant H_0 (the current expansion rate of the universe) through the time-delay cosmography
method. The SSZ framework does not modify these measurements because the lenses are in the
weak-field regime, but it provides a useful cross-check: any SSZ correction to the time delays would
systematicallybiastheinferredH_0. Theabsenceofsuchabias(theSSZandGRpredictionsagree
in the weak field) is a consistency requirement, not a discriminating test.
5.41.6 Signal Processing Applications
The additive decomposition has practical applications beyond fundamental physics. In satellite
communication, signals propagating near massive bodies experience a Shapiro delay that must be
accounted for in the timing protocol. The additive decomposition allows this delay to be computed
efficiently: the geometric delay (which depends on the signal path geometry) and the segment delay
(which depends on the gravitational field) are computed separately and added.
For deep space navigation (such as the Cassini mission, the Mars rovers, and future missions to
the outer solar system), the Shapiro delay correction is essential for precise tracking. The delay
for a signal passing near the Sun varies from zero (when the Sun is far from the signal path) to
approximately 250µs (when the signal path grazes the solar limb). This variation must be modeled
tonanosecondprecisionforspacecraftranging,whichcorrespondstoafractionalprecisionof10^{-5}
on the Shapiro delay.
The SSZ and GR (General Relativity, referred to asART in German literature) predictions for the
solar Shapiro delay agree to better than 10^{-12}, so the choice of theory does not affect deep-space
navigation. However, the additive decomposition provides a computational advantage: the solar
segment delay can be precomputed and stored as a lookup table, and the delay for any signal path
canbeobtainedbyinterpolationratherthannumericalintegration. Thisreducesthecomputational
cost of the tracking algorithm, which is important for real-time navigation.

| redshift | is the | difference |     | in clock | rates, | nothing | more. |

Analogy. Two musicians play the same note. One musician’s metronome runs slow (deeper in
gravity); the other’s runs fast (higher up). When the slow musician’s note reaches the fast musician,
it sounds flat — not because the note changed, but because the fast metronome marks more beats
per second, making the note’s oscillation rate seem lower by comparison.

| 5.49      | Historical    |       | Context  |     |        |                   |     |       |     |     |
The gravitational redshift was first predicted by Einstein in 1907, eight years before the complete
formulation of the general theory of relativity (GR). Einstein’s argument was purely kinematic: if
clocks run slower in stronger gravitational fields—as required by the equivalence principle—then
light emitted by a “slow” clock and received by a “fast” clock must appear redshifted. This line
of reasoning does not require the full machinery of curved spacetime; it follows directly from the
| equivalence | principle | alone. |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |
| ----------- | --------- | ------ | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The first laboratory confirmation came from the pioneering Pound–Rebka experiment (1960) at
Harvard University. Using the Mössbauer effect to measure the frequency shift of 14.4 keV gamma
rays over a vertical distance of 22.5 m, Pound and Rebka verified Einstein’s prediction to within
about 10 %. A later, more refined version of the experiment performed by Pound and Snider (1965)
reduced the experimental uncertainty to roughly 1 %, providing an even tighter confirmation of the
redshift formula.
The most precise test to date is the Gravity-Probe-A (GP-A) rocket experiment (Vessot & Levine,
1980). Inthismissionahydrogenmaserclockwaslaunchedonasub-orbitaltrajectorythatcarriedit
to an altitude of 10 000 km. The measured frequency shift agreed with the theoretical prediction to
70partspermillion, establishingabenchmarkthatstillservesasthegoldstandardforgravitational
redshift measurements.
Within the framework of Segmented Spacetime (SSZ), all of these experimental results are
| reproduced | exactly | in  | the weak-field |     | regime. | The | SSZ  | prediction |     |     |
| ---------- | ------- | --- | -------------- | --- | ------- | --- | ---- | ---------- | --- | --- |
|            |         |     |                |     |         | 𝑧 = | Ξ(𝑟) |            |     |     |

5.53.3 Worked Example: Pound-Rebka Experiment
The Pound-Rebka experiment (1960) measured the gravitational redshift of gamma rays over a
height difference of 22.5 meters in the Jefferson Tower at Harvard. The fractional frequency shift is
z = g h/c^2 = 9.81 times 22.5 / (3 times 108)2 = 2.46 times 10^{-15}. The SSZ prediction using Xi:
at Earth’s surface, Xi = r_s/(2 R_E) = 6.95 times 10^{-10}. The change in Xi over 22.5 meters is
dXi = r_s h/(2 R_E^2) = 2.46 times 10^{-15}, which matches exactly. In this weak-field regime,
SSZ and GR predictions are identical. The experiment confirmed gravitational redshift to 1 percent
precision; later experiments (Gravity Probe A, 1976) confirmed it to 0.007 percent.
5.53.4 The Redshift as a Counting Observable
The SSZ interpretation of the gravitational redshift is fundamentally a counting argument. A
photon with frequency f at radius r_1 has a wavelength lambda_1 = c/(f D_1), where D_1 =
1/(1 + Xi_1) is the local time dilation factor. As the photon propagates to radius r_2, it traverses
segments whose density changes from Xi_1 to Xi_2. The number of wavelengths that fit into the
photon at radius r_2 is the same as at r_1 (no retuning, Chapter 15), but the local wavelength at
r_2 is lambda_2 = c/(f D_2). The observed frequency at r_2 is therefore f_obs = f D_1/D_2 =
f (1 + Xi_2)/(1 + Xi_1).
In the weak field, where Xi is much less than 1, this reduces to f_obs approximately equal to f (1
- Xi_1 + Xi_2) = f (1 - Delta Xi), where Delta Xi = Xi_1 - Xi_2 is the difference in segment
densities. The fractional frequency shift is z = Delta Xi, which is the SSZ redshift formula.
This counting interpretation has several advantages over the standard GR derivation. First, it
does not require the machinery of Killing vectors and conserved quantities. Second, it provides a
physical mechanism (segment counting) rather than a mathematical identity (conservation along
null geodesics). Third, it naturally extends to the strong field, where the full formula z = (1 +
Xi_1)/(1 + Xi_2) - 1 applies, without requiring any additional assumptions.
The strong-field redshift formula makes specific predictions that differ from GR. At r = r_s (using
Xi_strong = 0.802): z_SSZ = (1 + 0.802)/(1 + 0) - 1 = 0.802 for a photon escaping to infinity. In
GR:z_GR=1/sqrt(1-1)-1=infinity. Thedifferenceisqualitative, notmerelyquantitative: SSZ
predicts a finite, measurable redshift where GR predicts infinite redshift and causal disconnection.
5.53.5 Solar Gravitational Redshift
The Sun provides the most accessible test of the gravitational redshift. The solar surface has Xi =
r_s/(2 R_sun) = 2.95 km / (2 times 696,000 km) = 2.12 times 10^{-6}. The predicted redshift of
solar spectral lines is z = 2.12 times 10^{-6}, corresponding to a velocity of z times c = 636 m/s.
This gravitational redshift must be disentangled from other velocity shifts: the solar rotation
(equatorial velocity approximately 2 km/s), convective motions (granulation, approximately 1
km/s), and oscillations (p-modes, approximately 0.5 km/s). The disentangling requires precise
spectroscopy of absorption lines from different regions of the solar disk and careful modeling of the
non-gravitational velocity fields.
Modern solar spectroscopy (using instruments like HARPS at ESO and the ESPRESSO
spectrograph at the VLT) achieves velocity precisions of approximately 10 cm/s, far better
than the 636 m/s gravitational redshift. The limiting factor is not the instrumental precision
but the systematic uncertainties from convective motions and line formation physics. Current
308

measurements of the solar gravitational redshift agree with the predicted value to approximately 1
percent.
For SSZ, the solar gravitational redshift is a consistency check, not a discriminating test. The SSZ
prediction z = Xi = 2.12 times 10^{-6} is identical to the GR prediction z = r_s/(2 R_sun) =
2.12 times 10^{-6} to the precision of any foreseeable measurement. The difference between SSZ

White dwarfs provide a stronger test of the gravitational redshift than main-sequence stars.
A typical white dwarf has M approximately 0.6 solar masses and R approximately 8000 km
(approximately the size of the Earth), giving r_s = 1.77 km and Xi = r_s/(2R) = 1.77/(2 times
8000) = 1.11 times 10^{-4}. The gravitational redshift is z = 1.11 times 10^{-4}, corresponding to
| a velocity | of 33 km/s. |     |     |     |
| ---------- | ----------- | --- | --- | --- |
This is much larger than the solar redshift (0.636 km/s) and is easily measurable with modern
spectrographs. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) has measured gravitational redshifts
for thousands of white dwarfs, and the results are consistent with the GR/SSZ prediction to
approximately 5 percent precision. The main source of uncertainty is the white dwarf mass-radius
relation, which depends on the equation of state of degenerate electron matter and the composition
| of the | white dwarf | (carbon-oxygen | vs helium | vs iron). |
| ------ | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | --------- |
For extreme white dwarfs near the Chandrasekhar limit (M approximately 1.4 solar masses, R
approximately 2000 km), Xi = 4.13/(2 times 2000) = 1.03 times 10^{-3}, and the gravitational
redshift is z = 1.03 times 10^{-3} (velocity 309 km/s). At this field strength, the SSZ and GR
predictions begin to differ at the 10^{-6} level – still unmeasurable, but approaching the regime
| where         | the predictions  | diverge. |     |     |

across multiple chapters. The validation chapters (26-30) show how this combination works in
practice and compare the resulting predictions with experimental data.

Can a photon change its frequency while it travels through a gravitational field? This apparently
simple question touches on a fundamental problem of gravitational physics: is the gravitational
red-shift caused by the photon losing energy during the transit, or by the difference in clock rates
| at the emission | and observation | points? |     |     |     |
| --------------- | --------------- | ------- | --- | --- | --- |
SSZ provides a definitive answer through an exclusion theorem: if a photon were to continuously
adjust its frequency to the local segment density during propagation (a process called “in-flight
retuning”), then the observed gravitational red-shift between any two arbitrary points would be
exactly zero. Because the Pound–Rebka experiment (1960), the operation of the Global Positioning
311

System, and Gravity Probe A (1976) all measure red-shifts that differ from zero, in-flight retuning
is experimentally excluded with high significance.
This result is not unique to SSZ—it holds in General Relativity and in any metric theory—but SSZ
makes the argument especially transparent through the operational frequency definition
𝜈 = 𝜙 /𝐷(𝑟) .

Why is this necessary? Every chapter in this book fulfills a specific function in the derivation chain
that connects the SSZ axioms ( 𝜙-geometry, segment density, two-regime structure ) with falsifiable
predictions. This chapter—Constraints on In-Flight Photon Retuning—answers a question that
cannot be resolved by the preceding chapters alone and whose answer is required by the subsequent
chapters. The material is presented at a level accessible to third-semester physics students, with
explicit motivation for each step and clear statements of what is assumed versus what is derived.
5.56.1 Pedagogical Overview
This chapter deals with a subtle yet fundamental question: does a photon alter any of its intrinsic
properties while it traverses a gravitational field, or is the observed shift in frequency entirely a
consequence of comparing the emission frame with the detection frame?
In the theory of General Relativity (GR) the answer is unambiguous. A photon that follows a null
geodesic carries a conserved energy
𝐸 = −𝑝 𝜉𝜇,
𝜇
where 𝑝 is the photon four-momentum and 𝜉𝜇 denotes the timelike Killing vector associated with
𝜇
the static space-time. Because 𝐸 is conserved along the geodesic, the photon’s intrinsic energy does
not change during its flight. The apparent change of frequency that an observer records is instead
a manifestation of the different rates at which clocks run at the point of emission and at the point
of detection. In other words, there is no “retuning” of the photon while it is in transit.
Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) must address exactly the same issue within its own conceptual
framework. The conclusion is identical: photons do not undergo any in-flight retuning. In SSZ
the density of space-time segments—characterised by the function 𝐷(𝑟) and the associated scaling
factor 𝑠(𝑟)—affects the coordinate speed of light along the photon’s trajectory. This modification
of the coordinate speed is a purely geometric effect; it does not alter the photon’s energy as
measured by any local observer. Consequently, the frequency shift measured by a detector is again
attributable solely to the comparison of the local proper times at emission and detection, not to
any intrinsic change of the photon itself.
The SSZ variables Ξ and 𝜙 that label the internal state of the photon, as well as the characteristic
radius 𝑟 that marks the transition between different segment regimes, are likewise invariant along

creation or annihilation of photons to compensate. Since retuning does not occur, the photon
number is conserved, the total beam energy is conserved (in the sense of the conserved Killing
energy), and the frequency shift is entirely due to the comparison of local clock rates.
This result has practical importance for photon-counting experiments in gravitational fields. Any
experiment that counts photons (such as a photon detector near a compact object) will record the
same number of photons as were emitted, regardless of the gravitational field between source and
detector. The energy per photon changes (because of the redshift), but the count does not.

Intuitively, this means: a photon traversing a gravitational field is like a ball rolling over a hill.
The ball speeds up going downhill and slows down going uphill, but its total energy (kinetic plus
potential) is conserved. Likewise, the photon “speeds up” (in coordinate terms) when leaving a
gravitational well and “slows down” when entering one, yet its conserved Killing energy remains
| constant | throughout | the transit. |     |     |     |     |

| 5.57.2   | Analogy: | The    | Metronome |          | on a           | Train |     |
A metronome ticks at a fixed mechanical rate (its intrinsic frequency). An observer on the platform,
whose clock runs at a different rate (due to relative motion in SR, or gravitational potential in GR),
measures a different tick frequency. The metronome did not change — the measurement standard
changed.
Gravitational redshift works identically: the photon’s intrinsic phase rate is fixed, but observers at
different Ξ have clocks that run at different rates, producing different measured frequencies for the
same photon.

The fact that GPS requires such a correction—implemented as a factory-set offset of the satellite-
clock frequency—provides a continuous, real-time verification that the photon frequency is fixed
at the moment of emission. Every GPS position fix, of which billions are performed each day
worldwide, independently confirms the exclusion (no-go) theorem of segmented spacetime.

The question of whether photons change frequency during gravitational transit has a rich history.
Einstein (1911) initially proposed that photon energy decreases during upward travel, analogous to
a ball losing kinetic energy. He corrected this view in 1916 with the general theory of relativity,
where redshift emerges from the metric structure rather than energy loss.
Schild (1960) provided the clearest thought experiment: imagine two identical clocks at different
heights, exchanging light signals. If the upper clock ticks faster (as GR predicts), then signals from
belowappearredshiftedsimplybecausefewerphotoncyclesarriveperupper-clocktick. Thephoton
does not change — the counting standard changes. This is the essence of the clock-comparison
