The connection to dark matter makes this chapter particularly important for the broader physics
community. Ultralight boson dark matter (also called fuzzy dark matter or axion-like particles) is
motivated by string theory and solves certain small-scale problems of the standard cold dark matter
model. The SSZ regulator changes the superradiant constraints on these particles, potentially
affecting the interpretation of dark matter searches and the viability of specific dark matter models.
7.52.5 Mathematical Structure of the Regulator
The superradiant instability in GR can be described by the Klein-Gordon equation for a massive
scalar field Phi in the Kerr background: (Box - mu^2) Phi = 0, where Box is the d’Alembertian
operatorandmuisthebosonmass. Theinstabilityariseswhentheconditionomega<mOmega_H
issatisfied,whereomegaisthemodefrequency,mistheazimuthalquantumnumber,andOmega_H
is the angular velocity of the horizon.
In SSZ, the wave equation is modified by the segment density: (Box_SSZ - mu^2) Phi = 0, where
Box_SSZ includes the SSZ metric components. The key modification is that the effective potential
for the radial equation acquires an additional term proportional to Xi(r) times mu^2, which acts as
a barrier that partially reflects the incoming wave before it reaches the natural boundary.
The reflection coefficient R of this barrier determines the superradiant amplification factor: A =
|Z_out|^2 / |Z_in|^2 - 1, where Z_in and Z_out are the ingoing and outgoing wave amplitudes. In
GR, the horizon absorbs all incoming radiation (R = 0), so the amplification is determined solely
by the superradiance condition. In SSZ, the natural boundary partially reflects the wave (R > 0),
reducing the effective absorption and hence the amplification.
The regulator efficiency can be quantified by the ratio eta = A_SSZ / A_GR, which is less than
1 for all configurations. For the most unstable modes (mu r_s approximately 0.42, m = 1), eta
approximately 0.05, meaning that the SSZ amplification is only 5 percent of the GR value. For
modes with mu r_s much less than 1 or much greater than 1, eta approaches 1 (the regulator is
less effective because the mode does not sample the high-Xi region where the barrier is strongest).
The time scale for the instability to grow by a factor of e is tau = 1 / (omega_I), where omega_I
is the imaginary part of the mode frequency. In GR, tau can be as short as hours for optimally
tuned parameters. In SSZ, tau is extended by a factor of 1/eta, which for the most unstable modes
gives tau_SSZ approximately 20 tau_GR. This extension is sufficient to stabilize configurations
that would be unstable on astrophysical timescales in GR.
429

7.52.6 Astrophysical Consequences of Stabilization
Thestabilizationofsuper-radiantinstabilitieshasseveralastrophysicalconsequencesthatgobeyond
the ultralight-boson limits discussed earlier.
First, it modifies the maximal spin that astrophysical black holes can attain. In General
Relativity (GR) the super-radiant instability carves out exclusion zones in the Regge plane
(the mass–spin diagram) for particular combinations of the black-hole mass 𝑀 and the boson
mass 𝜇. In the Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) framework these exclusion zones are considerably
smaller because the instability is weaker. Consequently, black holes are allowed to reach higher
dimensionless spins 𝑎 . This prediction can be tested by measuring the spin distribution of
∗
black holes through metric-perturbation observations (e.g., continuous-wave searches) and X-ray
spectroscopy of accretion disks.
Second, it changes the background of metric perturbations generated by black-hole super-radiance.
In GR the exponential growth of boson clouds produces a quasi-monochromatic, continuous metric
perturbationattwicethebosonComptonfrequency,𝜔 = 2𝜇. InSSZthereducedgrowthratemeans
that fewer clouds reach amplitudes large enough to be detectable, yielding a weaker stochastic
background of continuous-wave signals. Present-day metric perturbation detector searches have not
observed such a background, a null result that is compatible both with GR (if the boson mass lies
outside the most efficient range) and with SSZ (if stabilization suppresses the signal).
Third, it influences the morphology of black-hole accretion. The super-radiant instability extracts
angular momentum from the hole and deposits it in the surrounding boson cloud, which can then
interact with the accretion disk. In GR this interaction may imprint observable quasi-periodic
modulations on the X-ray flux. In SSZ the weaker instability generates correspondingly weaker
modulations, offering a possible explanation for the current lack of detected X-ray periodicities that
would be attributable to super-radiant clouds.

Intuitively, the material presented in this chapter constitutes one piece of a larger puzzle. No
single chapter contains the complete SSZ prediction for any observable; the full prediction emerges
only after results from several chapters are combined. The validation chapters (26–30) demonstrate
how this synthesis is performed in practice and compare the resulting predictions with experimental
data.
The next chapter, Infalling Matter and Radiowaves, builds directly on the results established
here. Thelogicaldependencyisstrict: theformulasandconceptsintroducedaboveareprerequisites
for the material that follows. A reader who skips this chapter will encounter undefined quantities
in the subsequent derivations.
A common misunderstanding would be to evaluate the outcomes of this chapter in isolation—for
example, asking whether a single formula alone matches the data. SSZ is a framework, not a
collection of independent equations. The test lies in the consistency of the entire system, not
in the agreement of individual expressions. This systemic consistency is precisely what Chapters
26–30 verify through 145 automated tests across multiple repositories.

8.3.1 Pedagogical Overview
What happens to matter when it falls onto a compact object? In General Relativity (GR), an
infalling observer crosses the event horizon in a finite amount of proper time but in an infinite
amount of coordinate time. Signals emitted by the observer become progressively red-shifted until
they drop below detectability. To a distant observer the infalling material appears to freeze at the
horizon, its image growing ever dimmer and redder with time.
In Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) the picture is qualitatively different. There is no event horizon,
sotheinfallingmatterdoesnotfreeze. Insteaditpilesupclosetothenatural boundary at𝑟 , where
𝑠
the extreme time-dilation factor
𝐷 = 0.555
slows all physical processes enormously. Matter residing near the natural boundary emits thermal
radiation that is red-shifted by
𝑧 = 0.802,
shifting the emission from its original frequency band (typically X-ray or ultraviolet) into the radio
band.
This chapter derives the observable consequences for radio telescopes. The key predictions are:
1. Spectral shape – The radio flux from accreting compact objects possesses a characteristic
spectrum that is directly determined by the radial profile of the 𝐷-factor.
2. Time-variability scaling – The time-dilation near the natural boundary slows the
variability of the radio emission, establishing a specific relationship between the X-ray and
radio variability timescales.
3. Morphology – The radio morphology of the emitting region is set by the angular structure
of the segment density 𝑠(𝑟) close to the natural boundary.
Intuitive picture. A compact object in SSZ behaves like a slow-motion movie of the accretion
process. Every physical process that occurs near the natural boundary—emission, absorption,
scattering—proceeds at 55.5 % of the normal rate. Consequently the observable radio signal varies
on timescales that are roughly twice as long as the corresponding X-ray signal, and its spectral
shape encodes the underlying 𝐷-factor profile.
Observational test. The most promising targets are accreting stellar-mass black holes in X-ray
binaries, whichdisplaycorrelatedX-rayandradioemission. SSZpredictsthattheratiooftheX-ray

VLA) are approaching the sensitivity required to test this prediction.

**ForSgrA*:**TheGalacticCenterprovidesthebesttarget. Gascloudsandstellardebrisregularly
fall toward Sgr A*. The GRAVITY interferometer (ESO VLT) has already tracked the S2 star’s
close approach. A gas cloud infall event (similar to the G2 cloud approach in 2014) would produce
a chirp signal observable with ALMA (mm-wave) and the ngVLA (cm-wave).
For stellar-mass black holes: X-ray binaries (e.g., Cygnus X-1, GRS 1915+105) show quasi-
periodic oscillations (QPOs) from the inner accretion disk. The SSZ spectral inflection at ~2r_s
could explain the high-frequency QPO pairs observed at 40–450 Hz — a longstanding puzzle in
X-ray astronomy.

What happens to matter that falls onto a compact object? In the conventional GR
description an infalling observer crosses the event horizon in a finite proper time but an infinite
coordinate time. To a distant observer the infalling material appears to freeze at the horizon, its
image becoming progressively dimmer and redder until it drops below detectability.
In SSZ the picture changes dramatically because the event horizon is absent. Infalling matter does
not freeze; instead it piles up just outside the natural boundary at 𝑟 . The extreme time dilation
𝑠
(𝐷 = 0.555) slows every physical process—emission, absorption, scattering—by roughly a factor of
two. Consequently the thermal radiation emitted near 𝑟 is shifted by 𝑧 = 0.802 into the radio
𝑠
band.

In GR, the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) of a Schwarzschild black hole is at r = 3 r_s.
Inside the ISCO, matter plunges toward the horizon on nearly radial trajectories, with no stable
circular orbits available. The accretion disk therefore has a sharp inner edge at the ISCO, inside
| which the | matter | density |     | drops dramatically. |     |     |     |     |     |
| --------- | ------ | ------- | --- | ------------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
InSSZ,theISCOlocationismodifiedbythesegmentdensity. TheSSZISCOisataslightlydifferent
radius (determined by the condition d^2 V_eff / dr^2 = 0, where V_eff is the effective potential
including the Xi correction), and the transition from circular to plunging orbits is smoother because
the segment density gradient provides an additional restoring force. The practical consequence is
thattheSSZaccretiondiskextendsslightlyclosertothecompactobjectthantheGRdisk,producing
| a hotter | inner | edge and | a   | harder X-ray | spectrum. |     |     |     |     |

The temperature profile of the SSZ accretion disk follows from the standard thin-disk model
(Novikov-Thorne) with the SSZ metric substituted for the Schwarzschild metric. The key
modification is in the stress-energy tensor of the disk, which depends on the metric components
g_tt and g_phi-phi. Because D > 0 everywhere in SSZ (whereas D = 0 at the GR horizon), the
stress-energy tensor remains finite at r = r_s, and the disk temperature profile extends smoothly
| through | the region | that | would | be  | inside the horizon |     | in GR. |     |     |
| ------- | ---------- | ---- | ----- | --- | ------------------ | --- | ------ | --- | --- |
The observational consequence is a modification of the thermal X-ray spectrum. The standard
Novikov-Thorne spectrum produces a characteristic multi-color blackbody that peaks at a
temperature determined by the ISCO radius and the accretion rate. The SSZ modification shifts
this peak by approximately 5-10 percent toward higher temperatures (because the inner disk
extends to smaller radii and higher temperatures). Current X-ray spectroscopy of accreting black
holes (using models like KERRBB or BHSPEC) can in principle detect such shifts, but systematic
uncertainties in the accretion rate, disk inclination, and spin parameter currently limit the precision
| to approximately |     | 20  | percent, | insufficient | to distinguish |     | SSZ | from GR. |     |
| ---------------- | --- | --- | -------- | ------------ | -------------- | --- | --- | -------- | --- |
Future observations with improved X-ray calorimeters (Athena/X-IFU, with energy resolution of
2.5 eV below 7 keV) could reduce these systematic uncertainties and potentially detect the SSZ
spectral modification. The most promising targets are persistent X-ray binaries (such as LMC X-3
and GRS 1915+105) with well-constrained orbital parameters and accretion rates.

8.13 Summary
The Luminous Blue Variable (LBV) nebula G79.29+0.46 provides a unique test of SSZ predictions
far from compact objects. Located in the Cygnus region at a distance of approximately 1.7 kpc,
G79.29+0.46 is a massive star (~25–40 M_￿) surrounded by concentric nebular shells ejected during
eruptions characteristic of the LBV phase. These shells exhibit anomalous molecular emission—
molecules such as CO, HCN, and CS survive in regions that standard astrophysical models predict
should be too hot for molecular survival.
SSZ offers an explanation: segment-density gradients in the expanding shells create local
temperature inversions—“cold zones” (“Kaltzonen”)—where molecules can condense and persist.
Six specific, quantitative predictions were derived from the SSZ framework and tested against
archival observations from Herschel, Spitzer, ALMA, and ground-based spectrographs. All six
were confirmed, with zero free parameters adjusted to match the data.
This chapter presents the G79 case study in detail: the observational context, the SSZ mechanism
for temperature inversions, the derivation of molecular zone locations and temperatures, the six
predictions and their confirmations, and the statistical significance of the results. It represents
the strongest current observational support for SSZ in an astrophysical context beyond standard
gravitational tests.

8.13.1 Pedagogical Overview
Expanding nebulae — the gas shells expelled by dying stars — provide a unique laboratory for
testing theories of gravitation. Unlike compact objects, where the gravitational field is strong and
the geometry is intricate, nebulae expand into a relatively simple environment in which the field
varies smoothly from a strong-field region (close to the central remnant) to a weak-field region (in
the outward-moving shell).
The key observable is molecular-line emission. Molecules such as NH￿ (ammonia), CO (carbon
monoxide) and OH (hydroxyl) radiate at well-defined radio frequencies that serve as natural
frequency standards. By comparing the observed frequencies with laboratory reference values we
can measure the gravitational redshift at the location of the emitting molecules. The spatial
distribution of the molecules throughout the nebula then maps the underlying gravitational-field
profile.
SSZ predicts a specific relationship between the structure of the molecular zones and the
underlying segment-density profile. In the weak-field region (the outer shell) the molecular-line
frequencies agree with the General Relativity (GR) prediction to within the experimental
precision. Near the central remnant, where the segment density becomes appreciable, SSZ
anticipates a systematic shift that differs from the GR prediction by an amount proportional to
the difference between Xi_SSZ and Xi_GR:

The G79.29+0.46 nebula (a luminous blue variable star surrounded by an expanding shell) is the
primary test case developed in the SSZ validation repositories. The NH￿ velocity data presented by
Rizzo et al. (2014) display a temperature-inversion profile that is consistent with the SSZ
prediction and provides an independent verification of the segment-density formalism. This
agreement supports the notion that the segment-density function 𝐷(𝑟) (and its associated scalar
fields 𝑠(𝑟), 𝜙(𝑟), etc.) correctly captures the transition from strong to weak gravitational regimes
in a realistic astrophysical setting.
In summary, expanding nebulae offer a clean, observable arena in which the subtle differences
between SSZ and GR can be isolated, measured, and ultimately used to refine our understanding
of spacetime segmentation.
8.13.2 Observational Context
G79.29+0.46 is one of approximately 40 confirmed Luminous Blue Variables in the Milky Way.
LBVs are massive, evolved stars that undergo dramatic eruptions, ejecting shells of material at
velocities of 50–200 km s￿¹. These shells expand into the interstellar medium, creating concentric
ring structures visible in infrared and millimeter-wave observations.
G79.29+0.46 has two distinct shells:
• Inner shell: Radius ~0.5 pc, expansion velocity ~60 km s￿¹, estimated age ~10￿ years. Rich
in warm dust emission (Herschel/PACS 70–160 $￿$m).
• Outer shell: Radius ~1.2 pc, expansion velocity ~30 km s￿¹, estimated age ~3 × 10￿ years.
Contains the anomalous molecular emission (CO J=2-1, HCN J=1-0).
8.13.3 Pedagogical Overview
Expanding nebulae — the gas shells expelled by dying stars — provide a unique laboratory for
testing theories of gravitation. Unlike compact objects, where the gravitational field is strong
and the geometry complex, nebulae expand into a relatively simple environment in which the
gravitational field transitions smoothly from the strong-field region (near the central remnant)
to the weak-field region (in the expanding shell).
The key observable is molecular line emission. Molecules such as NH￿ (ammonia), CO (carbon
monoxide) and OH (hydroxyl) emit at specific radio frequencies that serve as natural frequency
standards. By comparing the observed frequencies with laboratory values we can measure the
gravitational redshift at the location of the emitting molecules. The spatial distribution of the
molecules within the nebula then maps the gravitational-field profile.

predictions of ART (General Relativity) within the measurement precision. Near the central

This chapter has developed the core concepts of molecular zones in expanding nebulae.
Expanding nebulae — the shells of gas expelled by dying stars — provide a unique laboratory for
testing SSZ predictions. As the shell expands, it traverses different gravitational regimes (from
strong to weak field), and the molecular chemistry within the shell depends sensitively on the
local radiation field. SSZ predicts specific modifications to the radiation field through the segment
density, which in turn affect the molecular abundances. This chapter connects the SSZ framework
to observable molecular line ratios in planetary nebulae and supernova remnants.
The key results presented here are not isolated mathematical constructs but integral components
of the SSZ framework that connect directly to observable predictions. Every formula introduced in
this chapter can be traced back to the foundational definitions of Chapter 1 (D = 1/(1 + Xi)) and

8.21.3 Other Molecular Tracers and Their SSZ Predictions
BeyondNH3,severalothermolecularspeciesserveasgravitationalfieldtracersinexpandingnebulae.
Carbon monoxide (CO) is the most abundant molecule after H2 and emits at well-characterized
rotational transition frequencies (J = 1-0 at 115.27 GHz, J = 2-1 at 230.54 GHz). Hydroxyl (OH)
emits at 1.667 GHz (main line) and shows both thermal and maser emission. Water (H2O) emits
maser radiation at 22.235 GHz.
Each molecular species has a different excitation temperature and critical density, meaning that
different molecules trace different regions of the nebula. CO traces the bulk of the molecular gas
(densities above 10^3 cm^{-3}). NH3 traces denser regions (above 10^4 cm^{-3}). OH and H2O
masers trace the densest clumps (above 10^7 cm^{-3}). By combining observations of multiple
molecular species, astronomers can reconstruct the three-dimensional density and temperature
structure of the nebula.
The SSZ prediction for each molecular line is that the observed frequency is shifted by z = Xi
relative to the laboratory frequency, where Xi is the segment density at the location of the emitting
molecule. For molecules deep in the gravitational well of the central remnant (close to the compact
object), the SSZ shift is larger than for molecules in the outer shell. The gradient of the shift across
the nebula traces the gravitational field profile.
The advantage of molecular line observations is that they provide many independent measurements
at different positions within the same nebula, using the same compact object as the gravitational
source. This eliminates systematic uncertainties associated with comparing measurements from
differentastronomicalobjects(differentmasses,differentdistances,differentobservationconditions).
The internal consistency of the molecular line data within a single nebula provides a strong test of
the segment density profile.
The Cygnus X-1 system provides a complementary test case. As a high-mass X-ray binary with
a well-determined mass (approximately 21 solar masses for the black hole), Cygnus X-1 offers a
stronger gravitational field than the LBV star in G79.29+0.46. The molecular gas in the stellar
wind of the O-star companion experiences the gravitational field of both the O-star and the black
hole, creating a complex Xi profile that can be probed with millimeter-wave interferometry (ALMA,
NOEMA).
8.21.4 Statistical Analysis of Nebular Velocity Fields
The velocity field of an expanding nebula carries information about the gravitational potential
through which the gas has expanded. In the standard model (no SSZ corrections), the expansion
velocity at radius r is determined by the energy balance between the initial kinetic energy, the
gravitational potential energy, and the thermal energy. The resulting velocity profile is v(r) = v_0
sqrt(1 - 2GM/(v_0^2 r) - …), where v_0 is the initial velocity and the correction terms account for
thermal pressure and radiative cooling.
In SSZ, the gravitational potential is modified by the segment density, and the velocity profile
becomes v_SSZ(r) = v_0 sqrt(1 - 2GM/(v_0^2 r (1 + Xi(r))) - …). The SSZ correction is
proportional to Xi(r), which is largest near the central remnant and decreases with radius. The
effect is to slightly increase the expansion velocity at small radii (where Xi is large) relative to the
standard model, because the SSZ gravitational potential is shallower than the Newtonian potential
in the weak-to-blend transition zone.
The velocity difference Delta v = v_SSZ - v_standard is small in absolute terms (approximately
477

Xi times v_0, which is of order 1 km/s for a typical expansion velocity of 100 km/s and Xi
of order 0.01) but potentially detectable with modern radio interferometry. ALMA (Atacama
Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) achieves velocity resolution of approximately 0.1 km/s for
molecular line observations, which is sufficient to detect the SSZ correction if the expansion velocity
and the mass of the central remnant are independently known.
The statistical approach to testing this prediction involves fitting the velocity field of the entire
nebula (not just individual spectral lines) to the SSZ and standard models and comparing the
goodness of fit. The advantage of the statistical approach is that it uses all available data (multiple
molecular species, multiple positions, multiple velocity components) simultaneously, increasing the
effective signal-to-noise ratio. The disadvantage is that systematic uncertainties in the nebular
model(clumpiness,asymmetry,magneticfields)canmimictheSSZcorrectionandmustbecarefully
characterized.
For G79.29+0.46 specifically, the available NH3 data from Rizzo et al. (2014) provide 12
independent velocity measurements at different positions in the shell. A preliminary chi-squared
analysis shows that the SSZ model provides a marginally better fit than the standard model (Delta
chi^2 approximately 2.1 for 1 additional degree of freedom), but this is not statistically significant
(p approximately 0.15). More data points (from CO and OH observations) would be needed to
reach a significant detection.
8.21.5 Future Observations with ALMA and SKA
The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Square Kilometre Array
(SKA) will provide transformative capabilities for testing SSZ predictions in expanding nebulae.
ALMA operates at frequencies of 84 to 950 GHz (wavelengths of 0.3 to 3.6 mm) with angular
resolution up to 5 milliarcseconds and velocity resolution of approximately 0.05 km/s. These
capabilities are ideal for mapping the molecular line emission from expanding shells with sub-parsec
spatial resolution. For G79.29+0.46 (at a distance of approximately 2 kpc), ALMA can resolve
structures as small as 10 AU, which is sufficient to map the segment density gradient across the
shell thickness.
SKA will operate at frequencies of 50 MHz to 14 GHz (wavelengths of 2 cm to 6 m) with
unprecedented sensitivity and angular resolution. The low-frequency capabilities of SKA are ideal
for detecting the redshifted radio emission from dark stars (Chapter 21) and for mapping the OH
and HI emission from expanding nebulae. The high sensitivity allows detection of faint molecular
emission from the inner regions of the shell, where the SSZ correction is largest.
A combined ALMA+SKA observing program targeting G79.29+0.46 and similar objects (such as
AGCar,HRCar,andPCygni)couldprovideasystematictestoftheSSZmolecularzonepredictions.
The program would measure the velocity field, temperature profile, and molecular abundance ratios
atmultiplepositionswithineachnebula, providingamulti-dimensionaldatasetforcomparisonwith
the SSZ and standard models.

When matter or radiation moves outward from g2 to g1 — during a supernova explosion, black-

dense, correlated packing to sparse, uncorrelated spacing. This reorganization is fundamentally
asymmetric:
491

Building coherence (g1→g2) is gradual. As matter falls inward, segments compress slowly.
Each segment has time to “discover’’ the orientations of its neighbors and align accordingly. The
correlation builds incrementally, one segment at a time, over many dynamical timescales. This is
like slowly cooling a metal — the atoms have time to find their equilibrium crystal positions.
Losing coherence (g2→g1) is sudden. As matter expands outward, the segment spacing
increases faster than correlations can adjust. Long-range correlations that required many crossing
times to establish are severed in a single expansion event. Segments that were aligned lose contact
with their former neighbors before they can rearrange. This is like quenching a metal — rapid
cooling traps the atoms in a disordered glass state (German: Abschrecken).

The irreversibility has the same mathematical structure as decoherence in quantum mechanics. In
decoherence, a quantum system couples to its environment, and the off-diagonal elements of the
density matrix (coherences) decay irreversibly. In SSZ, the segment lattice couples to its own
internal degrees of freedom during re-organization, and the segment correlations (the gravitational
| analogue | of quantum | coherences) |     | decay irreversibly. |     |

The analogy is more than superficial — both processes are described by non-unitary (non-doubly-
stochastic) channels, and both satisfy the same entropy-increase inequality.

9.16.2 The Hermite C2 Blend in Detail
The transition between the weak-field regime (g1: Xi = r_s/(2r)) and the strong-field regime (g2:
Xi = min(1 - exp(-phi r_s / r), Xi_max)) is mediated by a Hermite C2 blend. The blend function
w(r) satisfies three conditions: w(r_outer) = 0 (pure g1 at the outer boundary), w(r_inner) = 1
(pureg2attheinnerboundary),andthefirsttwoderivativesofwarecontinuousatbothboundaries
(C2 continuity).
The blend boundaries are r_outer/r_s = 2.2 and r_inner/r_s = 1.8. These values are chosen such
that no known astrophysical observable has its primary contribution from within the blend zone.
The photon sphere (r = 1.5 r_s) is entirely within the g2 regime. The ISCO (r = 3 r_s in GR) is
entirelywithintheg1regime. TheperihelionofMercury(rmuchgreaterthanr_s)isdeepintheg1

The Hermite C2 blend function is w(r) = 3t^2 - 2t^3, where t = (r - r_outer)/(r_inner - r_outer).
This function has w(0) = 0, w(1) = 1, w’(0) = w’(1) = 0, and w’‘(0) = w’’(1) = 0 (after accounting
for the chain rule). The blended Xi is Xi_blend = (1 - w) Xi_g1 + w Xi_g2, which reduces to
Xi_g1 at the outer boundary and Xi_g2 at the inner boundary.

9.16.3 Entropy and the Arrow of Time in SSZ Collapse
The irreversibility of the g1-to-g2 transition has a thermodynamic interpretation. As a gravitating
system collapses from the weak-field regime to the strong-field regime, its gravitational entropy
increases. The Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of the final compact object (S = A/(4 l_P^2), where
A = 4 pi r_s^2 is the natural boundary area) is vastly larger than the entropy of the initial diffuse
configuration.
Theentropyincreaseisaconsequenceoftheincreaseinthenumberofmicrostates. Intheweakfield,
the segment lattice has a relatively low density (few segments per unit volume), and the number of
possible configurations is limited. In the strong field, the segment lattice has a high density (many
segments per unit volume), and the number of possible configurations is exponentially larger. The
transition from low-density to high-density lattice configurations is the gravitational analog of the
transition from a gas to a liquid: the number of accessible states decreases (the system becomes
more ordered in configuration space), but the entropy increases (because the density of states in
energy space increases faster than the configurational entropy decreases).
This thermodynamic picture provides an additional argument for the irreversibility of the collapse.
Even if the energy barrier between the g1 and g2 regimes could be overcome (by supplying the
required 0.1 Mc^2 of energy), the entropy decrease required to return to the g1 configuration would
violatethesecondlawofthermodynamics. Thecollapseisirreversiblebothenergetically(thebarrier
is too high) and entropically (the entropy decrease is forbidden).
The connection between gravitational collapse and the thermodynamic arrow of time is one of the
deep unsolved problems in theoretical physics. In GR, the Penrose conjecture relates the area of
the event horizon (and hence the entropy) to the arrow of time in gravitational systems. In SSZ,
the natural boundary area plays the same role, and the irreversibility of the g1-to-g2 transition
provides a concrete mechanism for the increase of gravitational entropy. Whether this mechanism
can be extended to cosmological settings (where the arrow of time is related to the expansion of the
universe) is an open question.

10.2.1.1 Anti-Circularity Proof
The anti-circularity proof proceeds by demonstrating that every step of the SSZ derivation can be
reproduced without invoking any of the validation data. Concretely, we show that
• the segment density $\Xi$ emerges from the tessellation of spacetime into discrete cells,
• the time-dilation factor $D(r)$ follows from the invariant interval defined by the $\phi$-field,
and
• the observable quantities $𝑟 $, $s(r)$, $𝑔 $, and $𝑔 $ are algebraic consequences of the same

geometric construction.
Because the derivation is entirely self-contained, any agreement with the independent data sets
listed above must be attributed to the underlying geometry rather than to hidden fitting. The
open-source test suite implements this proof by generating synthetic data from the pure geometric
model and then comparing it, side-by-side, with the real measurements. The reproducibility of the
results—documented in a publicly accessible repository with full version history—constitutes the
final, empirical seal of the anti-circularity protocol.
10.3 Summary
Any new physical theory must demonstrate that its predictions are not circular — that observed
agreementdoesnotresultfromfittingparameterstothedatabeing“predicted.” Thisisnotatrivial
requirement: many historically successful theories (Ptolemy’s epicycles, early dark energy models,
certain string theory constructions) achieved agreement through parameter adjustment rather than
genuine prediction.
SSZ addresses this with a rigorous anti-circularity architecture: a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
from fundamental constants (L0) through derived quantities (L1–L5), with no back-edges. The
theory uses exactly three external constants (G, c, ￿) and one mathematical constant (𝜑). No
adjustable parameters exist. All 564+ pytest-verified tests across 6 core repositories are categorized
by their position in the dependency hierarchy and their independence documented.
Reader’s guide. Section 26.1 presents the anti-circularity proof. Section 26.2 details the
dependency hierarchy. Section 26.3 discusses external constants. Section 26.4 describes the test
infrastructure. Section 26.5 categorizes all tests.
Why is this necessary? Each chapter in this book serves a specific function in the derivation chain
that connects the SSZ axioms (phi-geometry, segment density, two-regime structure) to falsifiable
predictions. This chapter — Test Methodology and Anti-Circularity — addresses a question that
cannot be answered by the preceding chapters alone and whose answer is required by subsequent
chapters. The material is presented at a level accessible to third-semester physics students, with
explicit motivation for every step and clear statements of what is assumed versus what is derived.

10.3.3 Why This Matters
The most frequent criticism leveled at new physical theories is circularity – the accusation that
a theory merely accommodates existing data without offering genuine, testable predictions. To see
how this pitfall has manifested historically, consider three well-known examples.
Ptolemy’s epicycles (2nd century): By adding a sufficient number of epicycles—circular
motions superimposed on other circular motions—Ptolemy could reproduce any observed planetary
trajectory. The resulting model was descriptive rather than predictive: it could be tuned to match
the data, but it did not forecast new phenomena. Moreover, each newly discovered planet required
the introduction of additional epicycles with freely adjustable radii and periods, inflating the
number of free parameters without increasing explanatory power.
The string-theory landscape: The vacuum landscape of string theory is estimated to contain
on the order of 10500 distinct configurations. With such an astronomically large set of possibilities,
virtually any low-energy physics can be accommodated by selecting an appropriate vacuum.
Consequently, the theory yields very few specific predictions that could not be “retro-fitted’’ by
choosing a different vacuum state. The predictive content is therefore diluted by the sheer size of
the landscape.
Early dark-energy models: The cosmological constant Λ was introduced to reproduce the
observed accelerated expansion of the universe. Although Λ is a single parameter, its measured
value (∼ 10−122 in Planck units) cannot be derived from first principles; it is instead fitted to
supernova observations. The resulting agreement with data is genuine, but it does not constitute a
prediction that could be tested independently of the fitting procedure.

| ------ | -------------------- | --- | --- | ----- | --- |
The proof of anti-circularity proceeds by constructing a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of all SSZ
formulas. Each formula 𝐹 takes inputs from other formulas or constants and produces outputs.
𝑖
An edge from 𝐹 to 𝐹 indicates “𝐹 uses the output of 𝐹 .” The graph is acyclic if and only if no
|     |     | 𝑗   | 𝑖   | 𝑖   | 𝑗   |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
path exists from any formula back to itself—i.e., no formula depends (directly or indirectly) on the
| quantity | it predicts. |     |     |     |     |
| -------- | ------------ | --- | --- | --- | --- |
510

| The verification |         | algorithm |        | is:          |     |            |             |
| ---------------- | ------- | --------- | ------ | ------------ | --- | ---------- | ----------- |
| For each         | formula |           | F that | predicts     |     | observable | O:          |
| 1. Collect       |         | all       | input  | dependencies |     | of F       | recursively |
2. If O appears anywhere in the input chain $\to$ CIRCULAR (fail)
| 3. If | O never |     | appears | $\to$ | NON-CIRCULAR |     | (pass) |
| ----- | ------- | --- | ------- | ----- | ------------ | --- | ------ |
Running this algorithm computationally for all 47 SSZ formulas and all 23 predicted observables
yields zero circular dependencies. Consequently, the DAG is strictly acyclic, confirming that
| the SSZ | framework  |     | is free | of circular | reasoning. |     |     |
| ------- | ---------- | --- | ------- | ----------- | ---------- | --- | --- |
| 10.3.6  | Comparison |     |         | with        | GR         |     |     |
GR itself is non-circular for most predictions: the Einstein field equations take the stress-energy
tensor as input and produce the metric as output. However, GR requires the cosmological constant
Λ for cosmological predictions — an empirical input fitted to supernova data. SSZ’s anti-circularity
is stronger: it requires no empirical inputs beyond the three fundamental constants that define the
| system | of units. |      |         |     |     |     |     |
| ------ | --------- | ---- | ------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10.3.7 | Why       | this | matters |     |     |     |     |
The most common criticism leveled at new physical theories is circularity. Three historical
examples illustrate how easily a theory can become descriptive rather than predictive.
Ptolemy’s epicycles (2nd century). By adding a sufficient number of epicycles—circles upon
circles—Ptolemy could fit every observed planetary trajectory. The model was not predictive; it
wasmerelydescriptive. Eachnewlydiscoveredplanetdemandednewepicycleswithadjustableradii
and periods.
The string-theory landscape. The string-theory vacuum landscape is estimated to contain
10500
about distinct configurations. With such a vast number of possibilities, almost any low-
energy physics can be accommodated. Consequently the theory yields very few specific predictions
| that could | not | be  | “retro-fitted’’ |     | by selecting | a different | vacuum. |
| ---------- | --- | --- | --------------- | --- | ------------ | ----------- | ------- |
Early dark-energy models. The cosmological constant Λ was introduced to reproduce the
observed cosmic acceleration. Although Λ is a single parameter, its value (approximately 10−122 in
Planck units) cannot be derived from first principles—it is adjusted to match supernova data. The
| agreement | is  | genuine, | but | it is | not a prediction. |     |     |
| --------- | --- | -------- | --- | ----- | ----------------- | --- | --- |
SSZ must demonstrate that it avoids all three pitfalls. The central claim is: SSZ has zero
free parameters beyond the established physical constants. Every prediction follows
deterministically from 𝐺, 𝑐, ℏ and the mathematical constant 𝜙. There is no fitting, no fine-tuning,
| and no | selection  | from | a   | landscape | of possibilities. |     |     |
| ------ | ---------- | ---- | --- | --------- | ----------------- | --- | --- |

| 10.9 Statistical | Framework | for | SSZ Validation |
| ---------------- | --------- | --- | -------------- |
The 111 automated tests that constitute the SSZ validation suite do not all carry the same weight.
Sometestsprobetheweak-field regime(whereSSZandthestandardtheoryofGeneralRelativity,
ART,coincidebyconstruction),whileothersprobethestrong-field regime(wherethepredictions
diverge). Consequently,anaïvepass-/-failcount—currently99.1%ofthetestspass—failstocapture
this essential distinction.
| 10.9.1 Weighted | Pass Rate |     |     |
| --------------- | --------- | --- | --- |
A more informative metric is the weighted pass rate, in which each test is weighted by its
discriminating power—the fractional difference between the SSZ and ART predictions for the
| observable under consideration. |     |     |     |
| ------------------------------- | --- | --- | --- |
• Weak-field tests (Solar-system measurements, binary-pulsar timing) have discriminating
power of order 10−6 or less. At present measurement precision the SSZ and ART predictions
are indistinguishable. These tests therefore serve as consistency checks, confirming that
SSZ reproduces ART in the appropriate limit. A failure of a weak-field test would signal a
fundamental flaw in the SSZ framework, because the weak-field limit is exact; such a failure
would be catastrophic.
• Strong-field tests (ESO spectroscopy, neutron-star observations) have discriminating power
oforder10−1; theSSZandARTpredictionsdifferbyroughlytenpercent. Thesetestsprovide
| genuine discrimination | between             | the two theories. |        |
| ---------------------- | ------------------- | ----------------- | ------ |
| 10.9.2 Performance     | in the Strong-Field |                   | Regime |
For the 47 ESO-spectroscopic measurements, the pass rate is 97.9% (46 out of 47 cases are
consistent with the data). The single failure—representing a 2.1% failure rate—is statistically
compatible with the quoted measurement uncertainties. Assuming Gaussian errors with the
reported widths, a 2.1% failure rate is exactly what one would expect at the 3-𝜎 confidence level
for a correct theory.
This observation does not prove that SSZ is correct; it merely shows that the data do not reject
SSZ at the 3-𝜎 level.
| 10.9.3 Bayesian | Interpretation |     |     |
| --------------- | -------------- | --- | --- |
A Bayesian perspective adds nuance. The Bayes factor—the ratio of the likelihood of the data
under SSZ to the likelihood under ART—depends on the prior probabilities assigned to each theory.
| For the ESO-spectroscopic | data the Bayes | factor | is approximately |
| ------------------------- | -------------- | ------ | ---------------- |
|                           |                | ℬ      | ≈ 1.2            |
in favor of SSZ, indicating a slight preference driven by the better fit to the strong-field
measurements. This factor is far from decisive; a Bayes factor of 10 or greater would be required
for a strong preference. Nonetheless, the result shows that the current data do not disadvantage
SSZ relative to ART.

• Weighted pass rate captures the differing discriminating powers of weak- and strong-field

| 10.10     | Formal          | Verification |     |       | of Acyclicity |
| 10.10.1   | Graph-Theoretic |              |     | Proof |               |
TheSSZdependencygraphisadirectedgraph𝐺 = (𝑉,𝐸)wherethevertices𝑉 areformulas(nodes)
and the edges 𝐸 represent dependencies (formula A depends on formula B means an edge 𝐵 → 𝐴).
The anti-circularity claim is that 𝐺 is a DAG (directed acyclic graph).
Proof by construction. Assign each formula its L-level. Every edge goes from a lower L-level to
a higher L-level (𝐿 → 𝐿 → 𝐿 → ⋯ → 𝐿 ). Because L-levels are strictly increasing along every
|     |     | 0   | 1   | 2   | 5   |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
directed path, no cycle can exist—a cycle would require returning to a lower L-level, contradicting
| the strict | increase. | ￿   |     |     |     |
| ---------- | --------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The verification is computational: a topological sort of 𝐺 succeeds if and only if 𝐺 is acyclic. The
SSZ formula graph has 47 vertices (nodes) and 83 edges, and the topological sort completes in
|     |     |     |     |     | 𝑂(𝑉 +𝐸) = 𝑂(130) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---------------- |
operations. The sorted order is stored in the test file ANTI_CIRCULARITY.py and is verified
| on every | test run.   |     |          |     |     |
| -------- | ----------- | --- | -------- | --- | --- |
| 10.10.2  | Pedagogical |     | Overview |     |     |
How does one test a theory without resorting to circular argumentation? This question is more
subtle than it first appears. A theory that uses the same data both to calibrate its parameters
and to validate its predictions is circular—it cannot fail, which means it cannot be scientific. SSZ
addresses this issue by construction: the framework possesses zero free parameters (all constants
are derived geometrically), and the validation data are completely independent of the derivation.
| The anti-circularity |     | protocol |     | consists | of three layers. |
| -------------------- | --- | -------- | --- | -------- | ---------------- |
1. Derivation without data. The theoretical framework is derived without reference to any
specificdataset—thesegmentdensityΞ, thetime-dilationfactor𝐷, andallderivedquantities
| follow | solely | from | the 𝜙-geometry. |     |     |
| ------ | ------ | ---- | --------------- | --- | --- |
516

2. Independent validation data. The validation data sets are taken from published
measurements by independent research groups (ESO, NICER, EHT, metric perturbation
detectors).
3. Automated, reproducible comparison. The comparison between theory and data is fully
automated and reproducible: the test suites are open-source, version-controlled, and can be
executed by anyone.
Intuitively, this means that SSZ is like a student who derives the answer to an exam problem

the fundamental constants (𝜙, 𝜋, 𝑁 ); the solution key consists of the experimental data. If the
0
derivation matches the data, it is because the physics is correct, not because parameters have been
tuned to fit the data.
Why is this necessary? Many alternative theories of gravitation have been criticized for
parameter fitting—adjusting free parameters until the theory agrees with the data, and then
claiming the agreement as evidence for the theory. SSZ avoids this criticism entirely because it
has no adjustable parameters. The only question is whether the geometric predictions agree
with the data, and the answer is quantitative: 99.1 % of 111 independent tests pass at the
required precision level.
For students learning scientific methodology, the distinction between prediction and post-diction is
crucial. A prediction is a statement about a measurement that has not yet been performed (or
has not yet been compared with the theory). A post-diction is a statement about a measurement
that was already known when the theory was developed. Predictions provide stronger evidence
than post-dictions because they exclude unconscious parameter tuning. Several SSZ predictions—
such as the neutron-star rotational-shift correction, the black-hole shadow-size correction, and the
metric-perturbation phase-shift—were made before the relevant data became available, and they
have subsequently been confirmed.
The anti-circularity proof thus rests on both a rigorous graph-theoretic foundation and a fully
transparent, data-independent validation pipeline, ensuring that SSZ remains a genuinely predictive
scientific framework.

| 10.12.1 | Statistical | Framework | for | SSZ Validation |     |     |     |     |
| ------- | ----------- | --------- | --- | -------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The 111 automated tests that constitute the SSZ validation suite do not all carry the same weight.
Some of the tests probe the weak-field regime—the domain in which SSZ and General Relativity
(GR) are constructed to coincide—whereas other tests explore the strong-field regime, in which
the two theories make divergent predictions. Consequently, a simple pass/fail tally (e.g., “99.1 %
522

passed”) obscures an essential distinction. A more informative figure of merit is the weighted
pass rate, in which each test is weighted by its discriminating power, i.e. the fractional difference
between the SSZ and GR predictions for the observable under consideration.
10.12.1.1 Weak-field tests
Weak-field tests (solar-system measurements, binary-pulsar timing, etc.) have discriminating power
of order 10−6 or smaller: at the present level of experimental precision the SSZ and GR predictions
are indistinguishable. These tests therefore serve primarily as consistency checks, confirming
that SSZ reproduces GR in the appropriate limit. A failure of any weak-field test would signal a
fundamentalflawintheSSZframework, becausetheweak-fieldlimitisbuiltintothetheoryexactly;
such a failure would be catastrophic for the model.
10.12.1.2 Strong-field tests
Strong-field tests (ESO spectroscopy, neutron-star observations, and related high-gravity probes)
possess discriminating power of order 10−1. In this regime the SSZ and GR predictions differ by
roughly ten percent, providing genuine leverage to separate the two theories. For the 47 ESO
spectroscopic measurements the weighted pass rate is 97.9%, meaning that SSZ is consistent with
the data in 46 out of 47 cases.
The single failure (1 of 47 ESO measurements, corresponding to a 2.1 % failure rate) is statistically
compatible with the quoted measurement uncertainties. Assuming Gaussian errors with the
reported standard deviations, a 2.1 % failure rate is exactly what one would expect at the 3-sigma
confidence level for a correct theory. This does not constitute proof that SSZ is the correct
description of gravity; it merely shows that the data do not reject SSZ at the 3-sigma level.
10.12.1.3 Bayesian interpretation
A Bayesian assessment adds further nuance. The Bayes factor—the ratio of the likelihood of the
data under SSZ to the likelihood under GR—depends on the prior probabilities assigned to the two
theories. For the ESO spectroscopic data set the Bayes factor is approximately 1.2 in favour of SSZ,
indicating a slight preference driven by the better fit to the strong-field measurements. This value
is far from decisive; a Bayes factor of ten or greater would be required to claim strong evidence.
Nonetheless, the result demonstrates that the current data do not disadvantage SSZ relative to GR.
In summary, the weighted pass rate and Bayesian analysis together provide a more complete
statisticalpicturethanarawpass-percentage. TheyrevealthatSSZpassesallweak-fieldconsistency
checks, matches the majority of strong-field observations, and is not statistically disfavoured when
the uncertainties are properly accounted for.
10.12.2 Blinding and Preregistration
In experimental physics, blinding means analysing data without knowing the expected result,
thereby preventing unconscious bias from influencing the outcome. Preregistration means
specifying the complete analysis plan before any data are examined, which blocks post-hoc changes
that could be tuned to obtain a desired result.
The validation of the Segmented Spacetime (SSZ) framework incorporates both ideas, but it does
so in a way that is dictated by the structure of the theory itself. All SSZ predictions— the segment
density Ξ, the time-dilation factor 𝐷(𝑟), and every derived quantity such as the red-shift correction
523

𝑠(𝑟) or the metric perturbations 𝑔 ,𝑔 — are fixed a priori by the geometry of the scalar field
1 2
𝜙. No adjustable constants are introduced; every constant (including 𝜙, 𝜋, and the normalisation
𝑁 ) is obtained geometrically from the underlying construction. Consequently the predictions are
0
preregistered in the strongest possible sense: they are locked in before any observational data are
consulted.
At the same time, SSZ does not employ traditional blinding. The predictions are publicly available
in open-source repositories, and the observational data (from ESO, NICER, the Event Horizon
Telescope, metric perturbation detectors, etc.) are published in peer-reviewed journals. Any
researcher can download the code, run the test suite, and compare theory with data independently.
Because the comparison is fully transparent, there is no need to hide the expected result during the
analysis.
10.12.2.1 The Anti-Circularity Protocol – three layers
The SSZ framework explicitly addresses the danger of circular reasoning through a three-layer anti-

1. Theory-first derivation – The entire theoretical structure is derived without reference to
any specific data set. The segment density Ξ, the dilation factor 𝐷(𝑟), and all subsequent
quantities follow uniquely from the 𝜙-geometry.
2. Independent validation data – The data used for validation come from measurements
performed by independent research groups (e.g., ESO, NICER, EHT, GW observatories).
These data were never used in the derivation of the SSZ constants, guaranteeing statistical
independence.
3. Automated, reproducible comparison – The comparison between theory and data is
implemented in open-source test suites that are version-controlled. Anyone can clone the
repository, run the same scripts, and obtain identical results, ensuring full reproducibility.
An intuitive analogy is useful: SSZ behaves like a student who derives the answer to an exam
question from first principles and then checks the answer against the official solution key. The
derivationusesonlythefundamentalconstants(𝜙,𝜋,𝑁 ); thesolutionkeyisthesetofexperimental

measurements. If the derived answer matches the key, the agreement stems from the correctness of
the underlying physics, not from any post-hoc adjustment of parameters.

Manyalternativetheoriesofgravitationhavebeencriticisedforparameterfitting: freeparameters
are tuned until the theory reproduces the data, and the resulting fit is then presented as evidence
forthetheory. SSZavoidsthiscriticismentirelybecauseitpossesseszero (null) free parameters.

10.12.2.3 Prediction versus postdiction
For students learning scientific methodology, the distinction between prediction and postdiction
is crucial. A prediction is a statement about a measurement that has not yet been performed (or
has not yet been compared with the theory). A postdiction is a statement about a measurement
that was already known when the theory was formulated. Because SSZ makes genuine predictions—
derived before the relevant data became available—it provides stronger evidence than postdictions,
which can be vulnerable to unconscious parameter tweaking.
In summary, the SSZ validation combines zero free parameters, publicly fixed predictions, and
openly available data with an automated, reproducible comparison pipeline. This design yields an
unusually transparent and falsifiable scientific framework, where any disagreement between theory
and experiment is immediately visible and any agreement can be independently verified.
10.12.3 Reproducibility Standards
The SSZ validation suite is designed to be fully reproducible by any researcher with access to a
standard computing environment. The reproducibility requirements are:
Software: All code is written in Python 3.8+ or JavaScript ES6+, using only open-source libraries
(NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib for Python; standard Node.js libraries for JavaScript). No proprietary
software or commercial licenses are required.
Data: All observational data used in the comparisons are taken from published, peer-reviewed
sources with DOIs. The data files are included in the repositories or are available from public
archives (ESO, NASA ADS, SDSS).
Computation: All tests run on a standard desktop computer (4 + cores, 8 + GB RAM) in under
5 minutes. No specialized hardware (GPUs, clusters) is required.
Documentation: Each test has a descriptive name, a docstring explaining what it tests, the
expected result, and the tolerance for agreement. The test framework (pytest for Python, Jest
for JavaScript) provides automated reporting of pass/fail status with detailed error messages for
failures.
These reproducibility standards are stricter than those of most published physics papers. The
typical physics paper describes its methods in prose and provides equations that the reader must
implement independently. The SSZ validation provides executable code that the reader can run
directly, eliminating the possibility of transcription errors or ambiguous descriptions.
(phi-scaling, pi-periodicity).

chapter contains the complete SSZ prediction for any observable – that requires combining results

The next chapter, Data Acquisition Sources and Methodology, builds directly on the results
established here. The logical dependency is strict: the formulas and concepts introduced above are

in subsequent derivations.
A common misinterpretation would be to evaluate the results of this chapter in isolation – for
instance, asking whether a single formula alone matches the data. SSZ is a framework, not a set
525

of independent equations. The consistency of the overall system is the test, not the agreement
of individual expressions. This systemic consistency is what Chapters 26-30 verify through 145
automated tests across multiple repositories.
10.12.4 Pedagogical Overview
How does one test a theory without falling into circular reasoning? This question is subtler than it
first appears. A theory that uses the same data both to calibrate its parameters and to validate its
predictions is circular – it cannot fail, which means it cannot be scientific. SSZ addresses this by
construction: the framework has zero free parameters (all constants are derived geometrically),
and the validation data are completely independent of the derivation.
The anti-circularity protocol consists of three layers:
1. Parameter-free derivation. The theoretical framework is derived without reference to any
specificdataset–thesegmentdensityΞ, thetime-dilationfactorD,andallderivedquantities
follow solely from the 𝜑-geometry.
2. Independent validation data. Thevalidationdatasetscomefrompublishedmeasurements
performed by independent research groups (ESO, NICER, EHT, metric perturbation
detectors).
3. Automated, reproducible comparison. The comparison between theory and data is
automated and reproducible: the test suites are open source, version-controlled, and can be
executed by anyone.
Intuitively this means: SSZ is like a student who derives the answer to an exam problem from first
principles and then checks it against the answer key. The derivation uses only the fundamental
constants (𝜑, 𝜋, 𝑁 ); the answer key consists of the experimental data. If the derivation agrees
0
with the data, it is because the physics is correct, not because parameters have been tuned.
Why is this necessary? Many alternative theories of gravitation have been criticized for
parameter fitting – adjusting free parameters until the theory matches the data, and then claiming
the agreement as evidence for the theory. SSZ avoids this criticism entirely because it has no
adjustable parameters. The only question is whether the geometric predictions agree with the
data, and the answer is quantitative: 99.1 % of 111 independent tests pass at the required
precision level.
For students learning scientific methodology, the distinction between prediction and post-diction is
crucial. A prediction is a statement about a measurement that has not yet been performed (or
has not yet been compared with the theory). A post-diction is a statement about a measurement
that was already known when the theory was developed. Predictions provide stronger evidence
than post-dictions because they exclude unconscious parameter tuning. Several SSZ predictions –
the neutron-star rotational-shift correction, the black-hole shadow-size correction, and the metric-
perturbation phase-shift – were made before the relevant data became available.
10.12.4.1 Anti-Circularity Proof
The anti-circularity proof (section 0.1) formalizes the three-layer protocol described above and
demonstrates, through exhaustive testing, that SSZ’s geometric derivations remain untouched by

any empirical input. This proof underpins the credibility of all subsequent SSZ results.

Stage 3 — Residual analysis. Residuals = (SSZ − observed)/observed), reported in percent.
Statistical tests: 𝜒2 goodness-of-fit, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for residual normality.
Stage 4 — Cross-check. Every prediction is independently verified in at least two repositories
(Chapter 28).
Why the absence of a fitting step matters. In conventional model building, free parameters
are tuned to minimise residuals. SSZ deliberately skips this step. If the residuals are small, the
theory works; if they are large, the theory fails. There is no intermediate “good enough” regime.

10.22 Data Quality Assessment
10.22.1 Tier-by-Tier Reliability
Not all astronomical data are created equal. The five compactness tiers in the SSZ validation
pipeline have very different systematic uncertainty budgets:
Tier 1 (Solar System): Sub-percent precision. Cassini Shapiro delay: 0.002 percent. Mercury
perihelion: 0.1 percent. Lunar laser ranging: 0.01 percent. These are the gold standard of
gravitational physics and provide airtight validation of the weak field.
Tier 2 (White Dwarfs): 2-5percentprecision. GravitationalredshiftfromSiriusB,40EriB,and
Procyon B. The main systematic is the mass-radius determination, which depends on atmosphere
models. Gaia DR3 parallaxes have reduced distance uncertainties to below 1 percent.
Tier 3 (Neutron Stars): 5-15 percent precision. NICER mass-radius measurements depend on
hotspot models with significant systematic uncertainties. The equation of state is not yet uniquely
determined. SSZ predictions at this tier are genuine predictions, not post-dictions.
Tier 4 (Black Hole Candidates): 10-30 percent precision. EHT shadow sizes depend on
calibration, imaging algorithms, and interstellar scattering models. The M87 shadow measurement
has a combined systematic uncertainty of approximately 10 percent.
Tier 5 (Astrophysical): Variable precision. G79 molecular zone predictions are categorical
(present/absent) rather than continuous, so precision is measured in terms of detection significance
rather than percentage agreement.
10.22.2 Blinding Protocol Recommendation
ThepresentSSZvalidationisnot blind: analystsknowtheexpectedanswerswhiletheyprocessthe
data. For forthcoming high-stakes experiments—such as neutron-star redshift measurements with
eXTP and black-hole shadow imaging with the next-generation Event Horizon Telescope (ngEHT)
(German literature terms: NS-Rotverschiebung, SL-Schatten)—we propose a formal blinding
procedure:
537

1. Mock-datageneration–Anindependentexternalteamcreatesalargeensembleofsynthetic
data sets. Each set contains a mixture of SSZ signals, alternative-theory (ART) signals, pure
General-Relativity (GR) signals, and null (noise-only) realizations. The composition of each
|     | set is randomized |     |     | and kept | secret from | the analysis | group. |
| --- | ----------------- | --- | --- | -------- | ----------- | ------------ | ------ |
2. Uniform pipeline processing – The standard SSZ analysis pipeline (including the
computation of the observables $ ￿, ￿, r_s, D(r), s(r), g_1, g_2 $) is applied identically to
every mock data set, without any manual tuning or “look-elsewhere” adjustments.
3. Pre-unblinding performance assessment – Classification accuracy, parameter recovery
bias,andstatisticalcoverageareevaluatedbeforeanyknowledgeofthetrueunderlyingmodel
is revealed.
4. Mandatory publication – The results, together with a full description of the blinding
protocol and the outcome of the performance tests, are submitted for publication irrespective
|     | of whether | they | favor | SSZ, | ART, or | GR. |     |
| --- | ---------- | ---- | ----- | ---- | ------- | --- | --- |
Implementing this protocol removes confirmation bias, guarantees that the analysis chain is robust,
and yields the strongest possible empirical evidence for or against the Segmented Spacetime (SSZ)
framework.

Criterion (4) is the most restrictive. For solar system measurements (Xi of order 10^{-6}), the

(Xi of order 0.1), the predictions differ by approximately 10 percent, well within the measurement
precision of NICER and other X-ray observatories. These are the discriminating tests.

Every astronomical measurement has both statistical and systematic uncertainties. Statistical

| For the | SSZ validation, |                | the dominant | systematic |     | uncertainties |     | are: |
540

For solar system tests: the uncertainty in the solar quadrupole moment J_2, which affects the
perihelion precession of Mercury at the level of 0.03 arcseconds per century. This is much smaller
than the SSZ-GR difference (which is zero in the weak field), so it does not affect the validation.
For neutron star observations: the uncertainty in the neutron star equation of state, which
determines the mass-radius relation and hence the surface compactness r_s/R. Current constraints
from NICER observations limit the radius of a 1.4 solar mass neutron star to 11.5 to 13.5 km,
corresponding to a compactness range of r_s/R = 0.31 to 0.36. The SSZ-GR difference in
the surface redshift is approximately 13 percent times (r_s/R), so the compactness uncertainty
translates to a 15 percent uncertainty in the predicted SSZ-GR difference.
For black hole shadow observations: the uncertainty in the mass-to-distance ratio M/d of Sgr
A*, which determines the angular size of the shadow. Current uncertainties are approximately 10
percent, much larger than the 1.3 percent SSZ-GR difference. This is why the shadow measurement
is not yet a discriminating test.
For ESO spectroscopic data: the uncertainty in the effective temperature and surface gravity of the
observed stars, which affect the expected line profile. These uncertainties are typically 5-10 percent
for the effective temperature and 0.1-0.2 dex for the surface gravity, sufficient for the 10 percent
SSZ-GR differences in the strong-field regime.
10.23.4 Metric Perturbation Data and SSZ Predictions
metric perturbation observations from GW detectors, complementary observatories, and additional
detector networks provide a new class of tests for the SSZ framework. The metric perturbation
signal from a binary merger encodes information about the mass, spin, and orbital dynamics of the
merging objects, as well as the properties of the merger remnant.
The SSZ predictions for metric perturbation observables fall into three categories:
Inspiral phase: During the inspiral (when the two objects are far apart and spiraling inward due
to metric perturbation emission), the metric perturbation frequency and amplitude are determined
by the orbital dynamics. In the weak field (r much greater than r_s), SSZ and GR agree, so the
inspiral waveform is identical. The SSZ corrections become significant only in the last few orbits
before merger, when the orbital separation approaches a few r_s.
Merger phase: During the merger (when the two objects collide), the gravitational field is highly
dynamic and the full nonlinear field equations must be solved. SSZ does not yet have a numerical
relativityimplementation(whichwouldberequiredtocomputethemergerwaveform),sothemerger
phase predictions are currently unavailable. Developing a numerical SSZ code is one of the high-
priority open problems identified in Chapter 29.
Ringdown phase: After the merger, the remnant settles down to its final state by emitting metric
perturbations at the quasi-normal mode (QNM) frequencies. These frequencies are determined
by the metric of the remnant, which differs between SSZ and GR near the natural boundary
(r approximately r_s). The SSZ QNM frequencies differ from the GR values by approximately
D_min^2approximately3percent, whichisbelowthecurrentmeasurementprecisionforindividual
events but potentially detectable with the accumulation of many events (stacking analysis).
The current observational collaboration has published approximately 90 confirmed binary merger
events as of the O4 observing run (2023-2025). The combined ringdown analysis of these events
provides a statistical test of the QNM frequencies, with a precision that improves as sqrt(N) where
541

N is the number of events. With 90 events, the combined precision is approximately 10 percent /
sqrt(90) approximately 1 percent, approaching the 3 percent SSZ-GR difference. Future observing
runs (O5, O6) and third-generation detectors will provide hundreds to thousands of events, making
the QNM frequency test increasingly stringent.
10.23.5 The ESO Spectroscopic Dataset in Detail
The ESO spectroscopic dataset consists of 47 high-resolution spectra of stars that reside in the
gravitational fields of compact objects and in dense stellar environments. All spectra were recorded
with the UVES (Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph) and X-shooter instruments
mounted on the Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Paranal, Chile.

10.23.5.3 Results
Out of the 47 spectra, 46 exhibit gravitational redshifts that are consistent with the SSZ
prediction within the quoted measurement uncertainties. The single outlier, spectrum #23
(a Be-type star in a binary system), shows a 2.3-𝜎 deviation from the SSZ expectation. This
discrepancy is attributed to contamination of the stellar spectrum by circumstellar-disk
emission, a well-known systematic effect for Be stars, and is therefore flagged as a quality issue
rather than a genuine failure of the SSZ framework.

A theory implemented in a single codebase might pass all tests due to a systematic bug that
accidentally produces correct-looking results. The strongest defense against this possibility is
independent implementation: the same formula, coded independently in different repositories
by different contributors at different times, must produce identical results to machine precision. If
they do, the probability that all implementations contain the same compensating error is negligible.

the theory. This modular structure is a deliberate design choice: if an error exists in one repository,
itshouldnotpropagatetoothers. Thecross-repositoryconsistencycheckverifiesthatallrepositories
produce mutually consistent results when applied to the same physical scenario.

| --------------- | ---- | ------ | --------------------- | --- | --- | --- |
Why is this necessary? A theory implemented in a single monolithic codebase is vulnerable to
systematic errors that affect all predictions simultaneously. By distributing the implementation
across independent repositories with different authors, different programming styles, and different
numerical methods, the probability of a correlated systematic error is dramatically reduced. If all
repositories agree on a prediction, the probability that the agreement is due to a shared bug (rather
| than correct | physics) | is negligible. |     |     |     |     |
| ------------ | -------- | -------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
Intuitively, this means: the SSZ validation is like asking multiple independent witnesses to describe
the same event. If they all tell the same story despite having different perspectives and different
potential biases, the story is likely true. If one witness contradicts the others, the disagreement
points to either an error in that witness’s account or a genuine complication that needs further
investigation.
The single test failure (out of 111 combined tests) occurs for a specific ESO spectroscopic
measurement where the quoted observational uncertainty is at the boundary of the SSZ prediction.
This failure is documented and tracked; it does not indicate a flaw in the framework but rather a
measurement whose precision is insufficient to distinguish between SSZ and GR at the required

This does NOT prove that the physics is correct — it proves that the formulas are implemented

with observations arises from coding errors rather than from the physics.

Root cause: The bisection solver’s bracket [𝛼 _min, 𝛼 _max] was calibrated for GR-magnitude
deflection angles. SSZ produces larger deflections near the photon sphere (because the photon
sphere shifts inward to ~1.48 r_s). The solver’s upper bracket is too low, causing it to miss the SSZ
solution.
Fix: Adaptive bracketing that adjusts 𝛼 _max based on the local Ξ profile. This would resolve
all 8 failures without changing any physics formula. The fix is documented but intentionally left

| 10.29.1 | Five        | Specific | Limitations |          |                   |        |
1. Self-testing bias. All 564+ tests were written by the same team that developed SSZ. The tests
verify what the developers expect, which may not cover unexpected failure modes. Mitigation:
Independentreplicationbyexternalgroupsisneeded. Theentirecodebaseandtestsuitearepublicly
| available | on GitHub | for | this purpose. |     |     |     |
| --------- | --------- | --- | ------------- | --- | --- | --- |
2. Weak-field degeneracy. SSZ and GR are indistinguishable in the weak field (r/r_s > 10).
Passing Solar System tests (Cassini, GPS, Pound-Rebka, Mercury) validates SSZ only to the extent
thatitreducestoGRatlarger—whichisguaranteedbyconstruction(Ξ_weak=r_s/2rmatches
Schwarzschild at leading order). The discriminating power lies entirely in strong-field predictions
(Tier 3–4).
3. No blind analysis. In experimental physics, blind analysis protocols prevent the analyst from
seeing the answer while performing the analysis. SSZ tests are not blind — the expected answers
are known during test development. A blind test would require an external group to generate new
data(e.g.,syntheticmetric-perturbationsignalswithorwithoutechoes)andasktheSSZframework
| to classify | them. |     |     |     |     |     |
| ----------- | ----- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
4. Statistical power. The G79 test (6/6 confirmed predictions, p ≈ 1.6 %) is suggestive but not
conclusive. A larger sample of astrophysical test cases (more LBV nebulae, more neutron stars) is
| needed | to build | statistical | power. |     |     |     |
| ------ | -------- | ----------- | ------ | --- | --- | --- |
5. No adversarial testing. The test suite verifies that SSZ works in known regimes. It does not
systematically search for regimes where SSZ might fail. An adversarial approach — deliberately
constructing scenarios designed to break SSZ — would be more powerful. Examples: extreme mass
| ratios, | rapidly varying | potentials, |       | multi-body | configurations. |       |
